memories.memory_text: I was in the editor's office when Mac reprimanded the reporters and assigned them to cover the Semple heir, demanding personal angles on his life.

grounded_facts: Mac expresses disappointment in Babe's lack of initiative, contrasting her current behavior with her past aggressiveness.
memories.memory_text: Mac called me out, asking what had gotten into me, and said he remembered when I’d do anything to beat Cobb—I felt his disappointment in my lack of initiative.

memories.memory_text: I used my reporting skills to negotiate a paid month-long vacation in exchange for getting information on the Semple heir, and I committed to delivering a major story that would fill the front page.

grounded_facts: Frank comments that Babe is crazy, indicating skepticism about her actions.
memories.memory_text: I heard Frank say, 'I tell you that dame's nuts,' and I knew he was talking about me, doubting my sanity.

grounded_facts: After Longfellow lifts her head, Babe opens her eyes and pretends to be confused, revealing she was not truly unconscious.
memories.memory_text: I opened my eyes and feigned bewilderment when Longfellow lifted me, making sure he thought I was just coming to.

grounded_facts: Longfellow offers his help and invites Babe into his house after she collapses.
memories.memory_text: Longfellow offered to help me and invited me into his house after I collapsed, saying he wanted to make sure I was all right.

grounded_facts: Longfellow expresses concern by asking Babe what caused her fainting.
memories.memory_text: I remember Longfellow asking me what happened, clearly concerned about why I had fainted.

grounded_facts: Babe tells Longfellow she has been searching for a job all day and has secured one starting tomorrow.
memories.memory_text: I told Longfellow I’d been walking too much while looking for a job all day, but I’d found one and would start tomorrow.

grounded_facts: Babe declines Longfellow's offers of help and claims she is fine, attempting to leave the scene.
memories.memory_text: I kept telling him I was fine and thanked him, but made sure to back away and decline his offers of help.

grounded_facts: After walking a few steps, Babe pretends to weaken again and falls against the iron fence, prompting Longfellow to rush to her aid.
memories.memory_text: I took a few steps and then let myself fall against the iron fence, clutching it to make it look like I was too weak to stand.

grounded_facts: Babe Bennett pretends to faint and collapses near a tree in front of Longfellow's house, initiating a staged encounter.
memories.memory_text: I pretended to be weak and collapsed near a tree in front of Longfellow's house, then fell against the fence to make it seem like I was really in distress.

grounded_facts: Seeing Babe's renewed distress, Longfellow looks around and calls for a taxi to assist her.
memories.memory_text: I saw Longfellow look around and call out for a taxi after seeing me collapse, just as I expected.

grounded_facts: A group of established poets, including Brookfield and Henaberry, gather at a round table in Tullio's restaurant for drinks and conversation.
memories.memory_text: I saw a group of established poets, including Brookfield and Henaberry, gathered at a big round table in Tullio's that the waiter said looked like a poodle.

grounded_facts: Brookfield rises to personally invite Longfellow to join the poets' table, prompted by the waiter's introduction.
memories.memory_text: I witnessed Brookfield rise to personally invite Longfellow to join the poets' table after the waiter introduced him as the man who inherited the Semple fortune.

grounded_facts: Longfellow directly calls out the poets for mocking him and expresses disappointment in their lack of kindness.
memories.memory_text: I told Mr. Brookfield I was disappointed in him, even though I thought his poems were swell, because making me feel ridiculous wasn't kind, and that wouldn't be good manners back in Mandrake Falls.

grounded_facts: Longfellow recognizes that the poets are making fun of him, leading to emotional hurt and a decision to leave.
memories.memory_text: I realized they invited me here just to make fun of me, and I felt hurt because it's easy to laugh at someone when you don't care about how much you hurt them. I decided it was best if I left, since I'd learned that not all famous people are big people.

grounded_facts: After deciding to leave, Longfellow returns to deliver two quick punches to Brookfield and Henaberry in retaliation for their mockery.
memories.memory_text: I saw Longfellow return and punch Brookfield on the chin with his left fist, then catch Henaberry on the jaw with his right.

grounded_facts: Morrow shouts 'Eureka!' and rises to follow Longfellow, showing respect for his integrity and courage.
Morrow, who remained silent during the mockery, expresses sudden admiration for Longfellow by exclaiming 'Eureka!' as he rises to follow him.
memories.memory_text: I saw Morrow, who had stayed quiet during the mockery, suddenly shout 'Eureka!' and rise to follow Longfellow, showing clear respect for his integrity and courage.

grounded_facts: In a drunken but self-aware gesture, Morrow invites Longfellow to punch him in the chin as a form of playful penance.
memories.memory_text: I saw Morrow, drunk but aware, dare Longfellow to hit him in the chin as some kind of playful penance.

grounded_facts: Morrow admits he has behaved like a 'skunk' and offers to symbolically punish himself by eating postcards at a newsstand.
memories.memory_text: I witnessed Morrow admit he'd been a 'skunk' and offer to eat postcards raw at a newsstand as a joke to make up for his behavior.

grounded_facts: As Morrow becomes increasingly unsteady, Longfellow repeatedly grabs his collar to prevent him from falling over.
memories.memory_text: I saw Longfellow grab Morrow's collar several times to keep him from falling over while Morrow was swaying and talking wildly.

grounded_facts: Morrow exaggerates the scope of the night out by claiming they will visit global landmarks like the Leaning Tower of Pisa and Mount Everest in a single evening.
memories.memory_text: I remember Morrow claiming we'd lean against the Leaning Tower of Pisa and climb Mount Everest in a single evening, as if it were really possible.

grounded_facts: After apologizing for his earlier behavior, Morrow enthusiastically invites Longfellow and Babe to join him on a wild night of drinking and exploration across New York City.
memories.memory_text: I was there when Morrow apologized for being a skunk and then invited Longfellow and me to join him on a wild night of drinking and adventure across New York, promising to show us sights we'd never seen before.

grounded_facts: A proposed evening of heavy drinking and social adventuring through New York City, led by Morrow, intended to introduce Longfellow and Babe to eccentric characters and surreal experiences.
memories.memory_text: I remember Morrow telling us about his plan for an evening of heavy drinking and wild adventures across New York, promising to show Longfellow and me surreal sights and introduce us to all kinds of eccentric people.

grounded_facts: Mac reads Babe's article about Longfellow Deeds aloud in his office, reacting with excitement to its content and impact.
memories.memory_text: I saw Mac reading my article aloud in his office, and I could tell he was excited by how his eyes lit up and how he emphasized the 'Cinderella Man' line.

grounded_facts: Mac praises Babe for creating the memorable nickname 'Cinderella Man' for Longfellow Deeds, recognizing its sensational impact.
Mac enthusiastically compliments Babe on the quality and sensationalism of her story about Deeds.
memories.memory_text: Mac told me he thought the 'Cinderella Man' nickname was sensational and that I was a genius, praising me for how memorable and impactful the story turned out.

grounded_facts: Babe discloses that she is posing as Mary Dawson, a stenographer, and has moved into Mabel Dawson's apartment to maintain her cover.
memories.memory_text: I told Mac that I'm posing as Mary Dawson, a stenographer, and that I moved into Mabel Dawson's apartment to keep my cover safe in case Cobb started snooping around.

grounded_facts: Mac instructs Babe to stay close to Deeds and produce daily exclusive stories to dominate the competition.
memories.memory_text: Mac told me to stay close to Deeds and send him exclusive stories every day, saying I could keep the other papers guessing while he'd report I was on vacation.

grounded_facts: When Mac moves toward her as if to kiss her, Babe sidesteps and reminds him their deal is strictly professional.
memories.memory_text: When Mac moved toward me like he was going to kiss me, I sidestepped and reminded him our deal was strictly for a paid vacation, not anything personal.

grounded_facts: Longfellow remembers Miss Dawson, a woman he tried to help, and expresses regret for not taking her home.
memories.memory_text: I remember Miss Dawson, a lady in distress I tried to help, and I feel regret for not remembering whether I took her home—I think I should call her to apologize.

grounded_facts: Longfellow regains consciousness after a night of heavy drinking, unable to recall key events, including losing his clothes and being brought home by police.
memories.memory_text: I can't clearly remember what happened last night—I only slowly started recalling things as I woke up, and I realize I don't know how I lost my clothes or how I got home.

grounded_facts: A private, chaotic morning session in Longfellow's bedroom where he confronts the consequences of his drunken night, receives urgent messages, and is confronted by Cobb about public image.
memories.memory_text: I woke up in my bedroom this morning after a wild night, disoriented and surrounded by chaos—Walter was there, I asked about Miss Dawson, and then Cobb burst in with a newspaper, confronting me about my public image, which I didn't understand.

grounded_facts: Miss Dawson contacts Longfellow by phone, marking a personal reconnection after his failed attempt to help her.
memories.memory_text: I remember when Miss Dawson called me, and I told them to give me the phone right away—she's the only one I wanted to talk to after everything that happened.

grounded_facts: Longfellow thanks Babe for showing him around New York, indicating appreciation for the experience.
memories.memory_text: I remember Longfellow telling me it was awfully nice of me to show him around New York.

grounded_facts: Longfellow expresses enthusiasm about the Aquarium, calling it 'swell' and suggesting he would visit daily if he lived in New York.
memories.memory_text: I saw how excited Longfellow was about the Aquarium—he said it was swell and that he'd go there every day if he lived in New York.

grounded_facts: Babe expresses that he would like to visit the Aquarium more often but is limited by his job responsibilities.
memories.memory_text: I told Longfellow I'd like to visit the Aquarium more often, but I have my job to think of, so I can't.

grounded_facts: Longfellow diverts the conversation by telling Babe she looks pretty tonight, avoiding her question about the opera board's decision.
memories.memory_text: I remember Longfellow telling me I look pretty tonight, right after I asked about the opera board's decision—he said it to change the subject.

grounded_facts: Longfellow reports that the opera board rejected his proposal to lower prices, cut expenses, and broadcast performances, calling him crazy and accusing him of wanting to run it like a grocery store.
memories.memory_text: I was told the opera board rejected Longfellow's proposal to lower prices, cut expenses, and broadcast the performances, calling him crazy and saying he wanted to run it like a grocery store.

grounded_facts: Longfellow leans in and asks Babe if she always wears her hair that way, indicating romantic interest and physical closeness.
memories.memory_text: I recall Longfellow leaning in and asking me if I always wear my hair that way, making me feel the closeness between us.

grounded_facts: Babe becomes aware that the public is ridiculing Longfellow with the nickname 'Cinderella Man' through overhearing passing girls and Longfellow's subsequent reaction.
memories.memory_text: I overheard those girls laughing and calling Longfellow the 'Cinderella Man,' and I could feel how uncomfortable it made me—and how he just glared after them in silence.

grounded_facts: After the girls mock him, Longfellow mutters that he would knock their heads together if they were men, showing repressed anger and gendered response to insult.
memories.memory_text: I heard Longfellow mutter that he'd knock their heads together if they were men, and it startled me—he sounded so angry, yet held back.

grounded_facts: Longfellow expresses violent frustration toward the journalist writing negative stories, saying he’d like to punch him in the nose.
Longfellow appreciates that Babe considers his feelings about the negative press, reinforcing emotional connection.
memories.memory_text: I remember Longfellow telling me he’d like to punch the journalist in the nose for writing those stories, and then saying he appreciates that I think about his feelings—it made me feel close to him.

grounded_facts: An intimate nighttime conversation between Babe and Longfellow while riding on top of a bus, covering personal feelings, professional challenges, and public perception.
memories.memory_text: I remember riding on top of the bus with Longfellow that night, talking about how he felt after the newspaper started mocking him, and how I wanted to ease the tension between us.

grounded_facts: To relieve tension, Babe shifts focus from the humiliating topic and suggests walking the rest of the way, prompting both characters to leave the bus.
Babe and Longfellow agree to get off the bus and walk the remainder of their journey, marking a joint decision to continue their time together in a more private setting.
memories.memory_text: I suggested we walk the rest of the way to get out of that tense bus, and I could see Longfellow agreed—it felt right to move somewhere quieter together.

grounded_facts: Babe encourages Longfellow to move toward Grant's Tomb, unaware of his emotional state.
memories.memory_text: I encouraged Longfellow to move toward Grant's Tomb, not realizing he was emotionally affected.

memories.memory_text: I remember that A group taxi tour stops at Grant's Tomb, where passengers observe the monument and engage in reflective conversation.

memories.memory_text: I remember that Babe asks Longfellow what he sees at Grant's Tomb, prompting his emotional and poetic response.

grounded_facts: Longfellow articulates an idealized, emotional vision of American history and possibility inspired by Grant's Tomb, revealing his deep patriotic sentiment and personal hope.
memories.memory_text: I remember that Longfellow articulates an idealized, emotional vision of American history and possibility inspired by Grant's Tomb, revealing his deep patriotic sentiment and personal hope.

grounded_facts: Longfellow's heartfelt speech affects Babe, who is fascinated and unable to laugh despite her initial impulse.
memories.memory_text: I watched Longfellow speak, and even though I first wanted to laugh, I couldn't—I was too fascinated by how sincere he seemed.

grounded_facts: After Longfellow's attempt to spit on Times Square fails and the wind blows it back on him, Babe laughs and wipes it off his coat with a handkerchief.
memories.memory_text: I laughed when the wind blew Longfellow's spit back on his coat, and I pulled out my handkerchief to wipe it off.

grounded_facts: A private nighttime conversation between Longfellow and Babe on the roof of a tall building overlooking Times Square, involving personal reflections and emotional tension.
memories.memory_text: I was with Longfellow on the roof of a tall building overlooking Times Square that night, and we had a private conversation where we shared personal thoughts and there was emotional tension between us.

grounded_facts: Longfellow acknowledges that negative articles about him will continue but claims he is no longer concerned.
memories.memory_text: I heard Longfellow say he wasn't worrying anymore about the negative articles, that they'd keep writing them until they got tired, and he asked if I believed all that stuff.

grounded_facts: Longfellow expresses confusion and sadness about why people enjoy hurting each other instead of trying to like one another.
memories.memory_text: I remember Longfellow looking sad and saying, 'Why don't they try liking each other once in a while?'—he was wondering why people enjoy hurting one another.

grounded_facts: Longfellow nervously asks if Babe is engaged, signaling romantic interest.
memories.memory_text: I remember Longfellow nervously asking me if I was engaged, like he was trying to find out if I was available without saying it outright.

grounded_facts: Babe asks why Longfellow doesn't go out with girls, prompting him to reflect on his isolation.
memories.memory_text: I asked Longfellow why he doesn’t go out with girls much, wondering if he really didn’t like any of the society girls he’d met, and I remember how he said they all seemed to have the St. Vitus Dance—awkwardly adding, 'Except you, of course.'

grounded_facts: Longfellow reflects on the emptiness of elite social life, comparing it to grand palaces without noblemen, indicating his alienation from the environment.
memories.memory_text: I remember when Longfellow told me about walking alone and thinking of Thoreau, saying the city built grand palaces but forgot to create noblemen for them—I could hear how disconnected he felt from all the wealth and glamour around us.

grounded_facts: Babe discloses that she comes from a small town similar to Mandrake Falls, creating a sense of shared identity with Longfellow.
memories.memory_text: I told Longfellow that I'm from a small town too, probably as small as Mandrake Falls, because I wanted him to know we shared something real.

grounded_facts: Babe recalls her childhood and her father, revealing emotional depth and drawing a parallel between him and Longfellow.
Babe tells Longfellow that he reminds her of her father, establishing deep emotional resonance.
memories.memory_text: I remembered fishing with my father and how he used to let me hold the line while he smoked, and I told Longfellow that my father was a lot like him—talked like him too—and that sometimes, for no reason, I'd go over and kiss him.

grounded_facts: Babe plays and sings 'Swanee River' using sticks on a bench, sharing a personal talent tied to her father's teaching.
memories.memory_text: I picked up some sticks and drummed on the bench while singing 'Swanee River,' remembering how my father used to let me hold the fishing line and how he'd talk just like Longfellow does.

grounded_facts: After Babe sings, Longfellow pretends disappointment, then offers to sing 'Humoresque' with her.
memories.memory_text: After I finished singing, Longfellow gave me a mock-disappointed look, then told me he could sing 'Humoresque' and suggested I start again so he could join in with me.

grounded_facts: Longfellow joins Babe musically by singing 'Humoresque' in harmony with her performance, creating a shared artistic moment.
memories.memory_text: I started singing 'Swanee River' again, and I heard Longfellow singing 'Humoresque' in harmony with my drumming, creating a beautiful, joyful blend between us.

grounded_facts: An intimate conversation between Babe and Longfellow while hidden in bushes, marked by emotional openness and mutual discovery.
memories.memory_text: I remember that quiet moment we shared hidden in the bushes, how I opened up about my father and singing 'Swanee River,' and how we ended up making music together—me drumming on the bench, him playing 'Humoresque' along with me, like we were in our own world.

grounded_facts: Longfellow and Babe sing together in the park, drawing brief attention from a passing policeman and being covertly observed by Bob and Frank.
memories.memory_text: I sang joyfully with Longfellow in the park, and we were having such a grand time together that I remember laughing with him at the end of our song.

grounded_facts: Seeing Longfellow's sudden action, Bob and Frank decide the evening is not wasted and begin actively filming again.
memories.memory_text: I was singing with Longfellow in the park when I noticed him suddenly look up and run toward the street; I think Bob and Frank must have decided to start filming again because of it, though I didn't see them directly.

grounded_facts: Mabel suggests they stop working and go to Joe's where others are waiting.
memories.memory_text: I remember Mabel telling me to knock off and go down to Joe's because the gang was waiting for us.

grounded_facts: Babe attempts to write an article while Mabel paints in her studio.
memories.memory_text: I was trying to write my article while Mabel painted in her studio, but I couldn't focus and ended up lighting a cigarette.

grounded_facts: Babe is unable to make progress on her article, showing frustration and emotional distress.
memories.memory_text: I felt completely stuck and frustrated, unable to make any progress on my article, and finally admitted to Mabel, 'I can't write it, Mabel! I don't know what's the matter with me.'

grounded_facts: Mabel notices Babe's distress and repeatedly asks what is wrong, showing care and concern.
memories.memory_text: Mabel noticed I was upset and kept asking me what was wrong, showing she cared, even though I tried to brush her off at first.

grounded_facts: Longfellow Deeds calls Babe, and she takes the phone from Mabel upon hearing his nickname.
memories.memory_text: I heard Mabel say it was the 'Cinderella Man' on the phone, so I grabbed it right away and said hello.

grounded_facts: Babe speaks sincerely on the phone, responding to someone about not sleeping.
memories.memory_text: I spoke on the phone and told the person I couldn't sleep either, matching their experience of being awake.

grounded_facts: Longfellow tells Babe that the poem he is writing is about her, using creative expression to communicate emotions.
Longfellow discloses he has been writing a poem about Babe, using poetry as a medium for expressing feelings he finds hard to say directly.
memories.memory_text: I remember Longfellow telling me he's been writing a poem about me because it's hard for him to say certain things out loud, so he puts them into writing instead.

grounded_facts: Longfellow thanks Babe for going out with him and expresses deep appreciation, indicating she compensates for past disappointing relationships.
Longfellow thanks Babe for going out with him and expresses how much she means to him compared to past relationships.
memories.memory_text: I remember Longfellow thanking me for going out with him and telling me how much I mean to him, saying I make up for past relationships that didn't work out.

grounded_facts: Babe responds emotionally to the news of the poem and expresses interest in reading it in the future.
Babe expresses her desire to read the poem Longfellow is writing about her.
memories.memory_text: I remember saying I'd like to read the poem Longfellow is writing about me sometime, after hearing he was working on it.

grounded_facts: Longfellow asks Babe when they will meet again and expresses enthusiasm upon hearing it will be soon.
Longfellow asks Babe if he will see her soon and reacts positively to her response.
memories.memory_text: I remember Longfellow asking me if he’d see me soon, and I could hear how happy he was when I let him know it would be soon—he said, 'Gosh, that's swell, Mary.'

grounded_facts: A telephone conversation between Longfellow and Babe, occurring in Longfellow's bedroom, where emotional intimacy is deepened.
memories.memory_text: I was on the phone with Longfellow in his bedroom, and I could feel how close we became during that conversation, especially when he shared that he writes poems because it's hard for him to say things directly.

grounded_facts: Mabel dismisses Babe's sentimental reflection, revealing her own vulnerability by referencing Charlie.
memories.memory_text: I saw Mabel shut down when I talked about the man's goodness—she told me to cut it out because I'd get her thinking about Charlie again, and in that moment, I realized she was guarding her own softness just like I am.

grounded_facts: Babe shares her confusion and growing admiration for a man whose sincerity challenges her worldview.
Babe expresses confusion and internal conflict about a man who seems either foolish or admirable, ultimately recognizing his genuine goodness, which contrasts with her and Mabel's cynical worldview.
memories.memory_text: I told Mabel that this guy might be the dumbest man alive or the grandest thing I've ever seen—I just can't figure him out. He said he wants to carry his bride over the threshold, and it made me realize he has a kind of goodness we don't see anymore, not in our world. I feel torn, like he's either a fool or something rare, and I'm struggling with that.

grounded_facts: Babe and Mabel engage in a reflective late-night dialogue about love, goodness, and professional cynicism in Babe's apartment.
memories.memory_text: I remember sitting with Mabel late at night in my apartment, talking about love and what it means to be good. We both started out wanting to be tough newspaper women, but that conversation brought up things we usually keep buried.

grounded_facts: Babe sits down at her typewriter, resuming her journalistic duties after a moment of introspection.
memories.memory_text: I sat back down at my typewriter, ready to get back to work after that moment of reflection—we’re all too busy being smart-alecks, competing for nothing.

grounded_facts: Babe makes the decision to leave immediately, unable to face seeing someone again, and begins packing her belongings.
memories.memory_text: I decided I just couldn't stand seeing him again, so I started packing my few things to leave immediately.

grounded_facts: Babe tells Mabel to fabricate a story about her sudden departure, claiming she got a job in China.
memories.memory_text: I told Mabel to say I got a job in China so he wouldn't know the real reason I had to leave suddenly.

grounded_facts: A tense emotional exchange between Babe and Mabel before being interrupted by Bob and Frank's arrival.
memories.memory_text: Mabel called me a fool and said I was acting like a schoolgirl when I told her I had to leave suddenly and asked her to tell him I got a job in China.

grounded_facts: Mabel criticizes Babe for her decision to run away, calling her a fool and dismissing her actions as immature.
memories.memory_text: I remember Mabel calling me a fool and saying I was acting like a schoolgirl when I told her I was running away.

grounded_facts: Babe confesses that continuing the deception is unsustainable and that the truth will eventually come out.
memories.memory_text: I told Mabel I didn't see any other way out, that keeping up the lie wouldn't work forever and he'd find out eventually.

grounded_facts: Babe cancels her date with Longfellow, indicating she is not going out tonight.
memories.memory_text: I told someone that my date with Longfellow was off because he was having a party at his house.

grounded_facts: Mabel pretends that Babe is Mary Dawson and that she herself is Mary’s sister, creating a false identity framework.
memories.memory_text: I remember Mabel pretending that I was Mary Dawson and saying she was my sister, setting up a false identity that I had to go along with in front of Longfellow.

grounded_facts: Longfellow Deeds arrives at the apartment looking for Mary Dawson, initiating a shift in the scene’s dynamics.
memories.memory_text: I was in the apartment when Longfellow Deeds arrived looking for Mary Dawson, and I saw how his arrival changed the whole mood of the room.

grounded_facts: Longfellow's unexpected arrival at the apartment to see Babe, leading to an impromptu outing.
memories.memory_text: I saw Longfellow show up at the apartment unexpectedly, and later I heard him say he threw out his party guests because they got on his nerves.

grounded_facts: Longfellow reveals he threw out the guests at his party to come see Babe, showing his prioritization of her over social obligations.
memories.memory_text: I remember Longfellow telling me he threw out his party guests just to see me, which made me feel uneasy.

grounded_facts: Babe quickly proposes going for a walk with Longfellow, possibly to escape tension or shift focus.
memories.memory_text: I suggested we go for a walk together to shift the focus and ease the tension I was feeling.

grounded_facts: Longfellow compliments Babe on her appearance, expressing admiration.
memories.memory_text: I heard Longfellow say I looked better every time he saw me, and I thanked him for the compliment.

grounded_facts: Mabel physically blocks Bob and Frank from leaving with their cameras, preventing them from photographing Longfellow and Babe.
Mabel blocks Bob and Frank from leaving to take photographs, asserting control over the situation.
memories.memory_text: I saw Mabel block Bob and Frank from leaving with their cameras, stopping them from taking any more photographs.

grounded_facts: Longfellow reveals his decision to leave and return to Mandrake Falls in a day or so, indicating a shift in his personal trajectory.
memories.memory_text: Longfellow told me he was going home, and I remember asking when—he said in a day or so, which made me realize his time here was ending.

grounded_facts: Longfellow reveals his lifelong habit of talking to an imaginary girl while hiking, symbolizing his longing for connection and foreshadowing his feelings for Babe.
memories.memory_text: Longfellow told me that when he used to hike through the woods, he’d talk to an imaginary girl to keep himself company, showing me how much he’s always longed for connection.

grounded_facts: A walk taken by Longfellow and Babe around the block, beginning and ending at the front steps of Babe's home, during which significant emotional revelations occur.
memories.memory_text: I walked around the block with Longfellow, starting and ending at my front steps, and during that walk we shared something deep—near the end, he held me in an emotional embrace.

grounded_facts: Longfellow hands Babe the completed poem addressed to her, asking only that she read it, not respond immediately.
Longfellow presents a completed poem addressed to Babe, expressing his deep love and emotional vulnerability.
memories.memory_text: Longfellow handed me his completed poem, told me it was for me, and asked only that I read it and not respond right away, and when I did, I heard him confess in verse, 'I love you, my angel - be mine, be mine,' which left me speechless and overwhelmed.

grounded_facts: Babe tells Longfellow goodbye with deep affection, affirming his reality and worth while releasing him.
memories.memory_text: I said goodbye to Longfellow, telling him not to let anyone hurt him and that he's too real to be broken, though my voice choked up and I felt the weight of how hopeless my love for him truly is.

grounded_facts: Babe reads the poem aloud, becomes overwhelmed with emotion, and ultimately embraces Longfellow.
memories.memory_text: I read the poem aloud, and my voice choked up—I couldn't even look at him until I folded the paper. I was overwhelmed, and even though I knew it was hopeless, I threw my arms around his neck and kissed him. I love him, but it scared me how much. When I pulled away, I was weeping softly, still caught in that ache of wanting something I can't have.

grounded_facts: After the passionate kiss, Babe realizes the hopelessness of the situation and begins to pull away from Longfellow.
memories.memory_text: I realized how hopeless this was, so I started pulling myself away from Longfellow, weeping as I freed myself from his embrace.

grounded_facts: After the emotional exchange, Longfellow leaves in a burst of joy, stumbling down the street.
memories.memory_text: I watched as Longfellow leapt down the steps in joy, tripping over a garbage pail and stumbling down the street, completely unaware of my sorrow.

grounded_facts: Mac initially reacts with excitement to the news of the proposal, imagining a news story.
memories.memory_text: I remember Mac getting excited when he heard about the proposal, shouting something like 'Cinderella Man Woos Mystery Girl!' as if it were a headline.

grounded_facts: Mac probes whether Babe has developed genuine feelings for the man she was assigned to investigate.
memories.memory_text: Mac asked me directly if I had fallen for the man I was investigating, and I knew he was trying to understand how I really felt.

grounded_facts: Mac suggests reassigning Babe to avoid facing the emotional fallout.
memories.memory_text: Mac suggested reassigning me to another job so I wouldn't have to face the man again, but I knew I couldn't take the easy way out.

grounded_facts: Babe resolves to reveal her true identity to the man who proposed to her, despite the emotional risk and potential consequences.
memories.memory_text: I decided I'm going to tell him the truth about who I really am, even though it's going to be hard and I don't know how he'll react.

grounded_facts: Babe announces her intention to leave the newspaper office, symbolizing the end of her current role and life chapter.
memories.memory_text: I told Mac I'm quitting the newspaper job and that I'll clean out my desk, because this chapter of my life is over.

grounded_facts: A private conversation between Babe and Mac in the newspaper office where Babe reveals her decision to confess her identity.
memories.memory_text: I had a private talk with Mac where I told him I'm going to confess my true identity to the man who proposed, and that I'm leaving the paper.

grounded_facts: Upon hearing the accusation, Longfellow grabs Cobb by the shirt-front, ready to strangle him in rage.
memories.memory_text: I saw Longfellow grab Cobb by the shirt-front, ready to strangle him in rage after hearing the accusation.

grounded_facts: Longfellow discovers that Mary Dawson is actually Babe Bennett, a star reporter who has been using him for stories, including coining his 'Cinderella Man' nickname.
memories.memory_text: I was told that Mary Dawson is actually Babe Bennett, the star reporter on The Mail, and that she used me for stories — including coming up with that 'Cinderella Man' nickname. I can't believe I was so fooled.

grounded_facts: Cobb confronts Longfellow, accusing him of being duped by Babe Bennett (posing as Mary Dawson) and exposing her true identity and intentions.
memories.memory_text: I was told that I had been deceiving Longfellow by posing as Mary Dawson while really being a reporter who used him for stories, even giving him the 'Cinderella Man' name.

grounded_facts: Babe gives Mac a loose-leaf book containing the names of all headwaiters in town, who can be sources of paid scandal.
memories.memory_text: I handed Mac my loose-leaf book with all the headwaiters' names, telling him he could use it to get scandal tips at good prices.

grounded_facts: Babe definitively rejects Mac's plea to stay, signaling her firm decision to quit.
memories.memory_text: I shook my head firmly at Mac when he tried to stop me from quitting, making it clear I was done.

grounded_facts: Mac tells Babe that others in her position always come back, implying she will too.
memories.memory_text: I heard Mac say that others in my position always come back, implying I would too, but I didn’t agree with him.

grounded_facts: Mac tries to dissuade Babe from quitting, expressing concern and disbelief.
memories.memory_text: Mac told me he couldn't let me quit and said I'd get the itch so bad in a couple weeks that I'd come back, even working for nothing.

grounded_facts: Longfellow receives a phone call via Cobb's relay.
Cobb transfers the phone to Longfellow so he can take the call.
memories.memory_text: I was told that Longfellow received my phone call through Cobb, who handed him the phone so he could take it.

grounded_facts: Babe initially greets the caller affectionately, then abruptly changes expression upon recognizing Longfellow's voice.
memories.memory_text: I started to greet the caller warmly, but I froze when I recognized Longfellow's voice on the phone.

grounded_facts: Babe begins a phone call, indicating she is about to leave and will arrive shortly, then attempts to explain something before falling silent.
memories.memory_text: I was on the phone, telling the person I was just leaving and would be there in a minute, and I started to explain why I did it, but then I just stopped—I couldn't go on, and I remember staring blankly at the receiver.

grounded_facts: The guard physically blocks Babe from entering the room after recognizing her.
memories.memory_text: I saw the guard hang up the phone and stand up quickly to block me from entering the room.

grounded_facts: The guard explicitly refuses Babe's repeated attempt to see the patient, stating it is the final refusal.
memories.memory_text: I was told by the guard, for the last time, that the patient didn't want to see me.

grounded_facts: Babe makes a final emotional appeal to the guard to at least pass on her name to the patient.
memories.memory_text: I made one last plea to the guard, asking him to at least pass on my name to the patient.

grounded_facts: The guard confidentially tells Babe that the patient only becomes agitated when her name is mentioned.
memories.memory_text: The guard told me confidentially that the patient only becomes agitated when my name is mentioned.

grounded_facts: Babe urgently appeals to Cobb to allow her to help Deeds by arranging legal defense.
Babe informs Cobb that she has secured Mac and is close to getting Livingston as legal representation for Deeds.
memories.memory_text: I caught up with Cobb in the corridor and told him I had to see Deeds and help him, explaining that I'd been all over town securing Mac and the paper's support, and that I could get Livingston too—someone who could give Deeds a real fighting chance.

grounded_facts: Cobb harshly blames Babe for destroying Deeds' spirit through sensational journalism.
Cobb confronts Babe and rejects her efforts to organize legal help for Deeds, accusing her of causing his downfall.
memories.memory_text: I reached out to help Deeds by organizing legal support, but Cobb stopped me cold, telling me Deeds didn't want any lawyers and blaming me for destroying him with my headlines.

grounded_facts: A legal proceeding where Deeds' mental competency is being contested, with Cedar pushing for institutionalization.
memories.memory_text: I saw the newspaper headlines about Deeds' sanity hearing, with Cedar pushing hard to have him declared incompetent and confined to an institution.

grounded_facts: Babe impulsively starts to rise upon seeing Longfellow, but Mac stops her with a hand.
memories.memory_text: I started to rise when I saw Longfellow, but Mac stopped me with a hand.

grounded_facts: Cedar formally requests to call Babe Bennett as the first witness in the hearing to prove Longfellow Deeds' insanity.
memories.memory_text: I remember when Cedar called me to the stand as the first witness, addressing me as Miss Louise - Babe - Bennett right there in front of the court.

grounded_facts: After Babe's outburst, the Judge warns her of arrest and orders her removal from the stand for disrupting court order.
memories.memory_text: After I spoke out, the judge warned me that another outburst would mean arrest, and I could feel the tension in the room as he ordered me to sit down.

grounded_facts: Cedar questions Babe about her employment and authorship of articles on Deeds, attempting to establish credibility for the prosecution's case.
memories.memory_text: I was questioned about my job at the Morning Mail and whether I'd been assigned to follow Deeds, and I knew they were trying to use my past work against him.

grounded_facts: Babe, under oath, openly defies Cedar's questioning by rejecting the truth of her own articles and accusing the court of a frameup.
Babe directly challenges the legitimacy of the hearing, accusing it of being a frameup and demanding to be heard.
memories.memory_text: I stood up under oath and rejected my own articles, telling the court this was a frameup and that I had a right to be heard, just like any expert.

grounded_facts: When asked by the judge if he has anything to say in defense of the allegations, Longfellow Deeds remains silent.
memories.memory_text: I watched Deeds when the judge asked him if he had anything to say in defense—he stayed silent, just shook his head, and I felt my hope slipping.

grounded_facts: A formal legal proceeding in a courtroom to determine whether Longfellow Deeds is mentally fit to manage his inherited fortune, involving witness testimony, expert diagnosis, public sentiment, and moral confrontation.
memories.memory_text: I realized this whole proceeding was meant to prove Deeds was unfit to manage the Semple fortune, using testimony and psychiatrists to paint him as insane.

grounded_facts: Despite Babe's retraction, Cedar submits her articles as evidence, and the judge marks them Exhibit A for the plaintiff.
memories.memory_text: Even after I retracted everything, I saw Cedar submit my articles as evidence and heard the judge mark them Exhibit A for the plaintiff.

grounded_facts: After Babe is dismissed, Mac places an affectionate arm around her shoulders as she returns to her seat.
memories.memory_text: After I was dismissed, I remember Mac putting an affectionate arm around my shoulders as I returned to my seat, a small comfort in that moment.

grounded_facts: A psychiatrist clarifies for the court that 'pixilated' is an old American term meaning someone is mentally unbalanced, equivalent to being 'balmy.'
memories.memory_text: I was in the courtroom when the psychiatrist explained that 'pixilated' is an old American term meaning someone is mentally unbalanced, like saying a person is 'balmy.'

grounded_facts: Cedar questions the Falkner sisters about their knowledge of Deeds, guiding them to confirm community belief in his instability.
memories.memory_text: I was in the courtroom when Cedar questioned the Falkner sisters, guiding them to confirm that everyone back home thought Longfellow Deeds was unstable.

grounded_facts: A series of witnesses — including a policeman, waiter, Madame Pomponi, bodyguards, and a cabman — recount incidents where Deeds acted unpredictably, such as cleaning a restaurant, ejecting performers, dismissing bodyguards, and feeding doughnuts to a horse.
memories.memory_text: I heard a waiter say Deeds was mopping floors, and bodyguards claimed he threw them out — one even said he fed doughnuts to a horse named Clara, which made her refuse to eat anything else.

grounded_facts: Cedar presents photographic enlargements of Deeds's antics and has them authenticated by the photographer.
Cedar presents enlarged photographs of Deeds engaging in unusual behavior, authenticated by Bob, the photographer who took the original images.
memories.memory_text: I saw Cedar present enlarged photos of Deeds acting strangely, and the photographer, Bob, confirmed he took the originals, saying he often photographs people who act like nuts.

grounded_facts: Dr. Emil Von Holler testifies that Longfellow Deeds suffers from manic depression, explaining the condition using a mood chart and linking Deeds's behaviors — such as hosting a reception and then throwing guests out — to mood cycles.
Dr. Von Holler uses a mood chart to explain manic depression and applies it directly to Deeds's behavior, asserting he is mentally ill.
memories.memory_text: I watched Dr. Von Holler testify that Deeds suffers from manic depression, using a mood chart on the blackboard to explain how his behavior — like throwing guests out when depressed — fits the cycle.

grounded_facts: After presenting all evidence and expert testimony, Cedar formally concludes the prosecution's presentation in the insanity hearing.
memories.memory_text: I remember when Cedar finished presenting all the evidence and simply said, 'Your Honor, we rest,' marking the end of the prosecution's case.

grounded_facts: Babe leans close to Longfellow and pleads with him to speak, expressing remorse and love.
memories.memory_text: I leaned close to Longfellow and pleaded with him to speak, telling him I knew how horrible I'd been and that no matter what happened, I needed him to do this for me.

grounded_facts: Babe Bennett interrupts the court's decision process, insisting that Longfellow Deeds must be given a chance to defend himself before being committed.
memories.memory_text: I interrupted the court because I couldn't let them commit Deeds without making him talk first—I ran up to the judge and insisted he must be allowed to defend himself before any decision was made, then I sat down in the witness stand.

grounded_facts: Babe Bennett testifies that Deeds is not insane but has been victimized by the press and herself, arguing that his honesty makes him appear crazy in a corrupt world.
memories.memory_text: I testified that Deeds isn't insane but has been hurt by everyone he met, especially me, and that the newspapers turned him into a joke; I said his honesty makes him seem crazy in a world that can't handle the truth.

grounded_facts: Cedar attempts to discredit Babe by claiming she is in love with Deeds; Babe defiantly admits it but insists it doesn't invalidate her truth.
memories.memory_text: I was standing in the courtroom when Cedar accused me of being in love with Deeds, trying to undermine my credibility; I defiantly admitted it with a 'Yes!!!' because I knew my feelings didn't make my testimony any less true.

grounded_facts: Mac, Babe's editor, confirms that Babe quit her job out of respect for Deeds and endorses her account, adding institutional credibility.
Mac publicly backs Babe's account and affirms Deeds's character, nudging Deeds to speak.
memories.memory_text: I remember Mac, my editor, standing up and confirming what I said in court—he told the judge that when I quit, I spoke about what a swell fellow Deeds was, and that anything I say is okay with him, then he urged Deeds directly not to be a sucker and to stand up and speak his piece.

grounded_facts: Farmers and townspeople in the audience rise up, demanding that Deeds speak and declaring their support, showing collective solidarity.
memories.memory_text: I saw the farmers and townspeople in the audience rise up, shouting at Mr. Deeds to speak and declaring their support, saying they wouldn't let him be framed.

grounded_facts: Longfellow defends normalcy by pointing out common 'odd' behaviors like doodling and O-filling, using the Judge and Dr. Von Holler as examples.
memories.memory_text: I saw Longfellow defend himself by saying that playing the tuba helps him think, and that everyone has little odd habits—like how the Judge fills in the O's on paper, which made the courtroom laugh when he pointed it out.

grounded_facts: Longfellow exposes Dr. Von Holler's doodling as a 'foolish' habit, undermining his expert status by equating it with tuba playing.
memories.memory_text: I watched Longfellow expose Dr. Von Holler’s doodling as a foolish habit, picking up the paper he was scribbling on and calling it out just like tuba playing, which made the spectators roar with laughter.

grounded_facts: Longfellow hands a doodle resembling Cedar to the judge, inviting ridicule and undermining Cedar's dignity.
memories.memory_text: I saw Longfellow hand a doodle of Mr. Cedar to the judge, making everyone laugh and pointing out how even authority figures have odd habits, which embarrassed them but made me realize how unfair they were being.

grounded_facts: Longfellow acknowledges being drunk during past incidents, attributing his actions to a one-time lapse rather than insanity.
memories.memory_text: I heard Longfellow admit in court that he was drunk during those incidents, saying it was the first time he'd ever been drunk and that he didn't remember what happened.

grounded_facts: Longfellow uses a doodle of Mr. Cedar to illustrate that everyone, including authority figures, engages in odd behaviors, normalizing his own eccentricities.
memories.memory_text: I remember Longfellow using that doodle of Mr. Cedar to show that everyone has strange little behaviors, even people like Dr. Von Holler or Mr. Semple, and I thought to myself that it was smart how he used it to defend himself by making his own actions seem normal.

grounded_facts: Longfellow points out that Cedar's son was also drunk and acted recklessly, undermining Cedar's moral authority.
Longfellow directly questions Cedar about his son's drunken behavior, challenging his moral standing.
memories.memory_text: I saw Longfellow challenge Cedar about his son's drunken behavior, pointing out how he got drunk and drove a taxi while the driver sat inside, and he directly questioned Cedar about it to undermine his moral authority.

grounded_facts: Longfellow confirms that the Falkner sisters live rent-free in a house he owns, demonstrating generosity and undermining claims of irrationality.
memories.memory_text: I heard Longfellow ask Jane and Amy if they paid rent on the house he owns, and they both said no, they never pay any rent.

grounded_facts: Longfellow asks Jane who in Mandrake Falls is 'pixilated,' leading to the conclusion that everyone is except the sisters themselves.
memories.memory_text: I remember Longfellow asking Jane who in Mandrake Falls was 'pixilated,' and she said everybody was except the two sisters themselves.

grounded_facts: The Falkner sisters collectively testify that the townspeople believe Longfellow Deeds is 'pixilated,' citing his odd behaviors such as walking in the rain without a hat, talking to himself, and violently confronting Chuck Dillon.
memories.memory_text: I heard the Falkner sisters say the townspeople believed Deeds was 'pixilated' because he walked in the rain without a hat, talked to himself, and had a violent encounter with Chuck Dillon.

grounded_facts: Longfellow explains his desire to distribute his wealth as an effort to help struggling people, framing it as moral responsibility rather than madness.
memories.memory_text: I heard Longfellow explain that helping struggling people with his money was like aiding cars that can't make it up a steep hill—he saw it as a moral duty, not madness.

grounded_facts: Longfellow calls on applicants for farms to stand, visually demonstrating who he intends to help.
memories.memory_text: I saw Longfellow call on the farm applicants to stand up so everyone could see who he was trying to help—he pointed them out and said they were the ones who needed it.

grounded_facts: Longfellow outlines his structured plan to give land and resources to struggling families, framing it as rational and morally justified.
memories.memory_text: I heard Longfellow explain his plan to give ten acres, a horse, a cow, and seed to each family, and how he believed it was fair and reasonable if they worked the farm for three years.

grounded_facts: Longfellow claims Cedar does not genuinely believe he is insane, pointing out that Cedar offered to drop the case if financially compensated, thus revealing self-interest over concern for public welfare.
memories.memory_text: I remember Longfellow saying that Cedar had offered to drop the case if he was paid off, which proved to me that Cedar wasn't really concerned about his sanity but only about money.

grounded_facts: Cedar interrupts the proceedings to call Longfellow's proposal 'colossally stupid' and an 'insult to intelligence,' escalating personal conflict.
memories.memory_text: I saw Cedar interrupt and call Longfellow's idea 'colossally stupid' and an 'insult to our intelligence,' which made the tension in the room unbearable.

grounded_facts: After remaining silent, Longfellow Deeds finally speaks up, requesting to give his side of the story in response to the public support and Babe's plea.
memories.memory_text: I saw Longfellow finally speak up in court after staying silent, asking to give his side because of the public support and my plea.

grounded_facts: Longfellow physically assaults Cedar after accusing him of hypocrisy and attempting to block his philanthropic plan, marking a climactic breakdown of decorum and restraint.
memories.memory_text: I watched in shock as Longfellow stood up and punched Cedar right on the jaw after all the accusations and insults.

grounded_facts: The judge delivers the final verdict in Mr. Deeds' sanity hearing, concluding the trial.
The judge declares Mr. Deeds sane and dismisses the case, reversing the expected outcome.
The judge publicly acknowledges Longfellow's role by clasping his hand after the verdict.
memories.memory_text: I heard the judge speak about Longfellow's strange behavior, but then he surprised everyone by declaring him the sanest man in the courtroom and dismissing the case—I saw him smile and clasp Longfellow's hand right after.

grounded_facts: Mrs. Semple slaps her husband in anger after the verdict goes against their interests.
memories.memory_text: I saw Mrs. Semple turn to her husband and slap him right after the verdict was read, her face full of anger and disappointment.

grounded_facts: Budington confronts Cedar, accusing him of orchestrating a failed scheme.
memories.memory_text: I watched Budington stand up and confront Cedar, shouting 'I knew it!' before Cedar pushed him aside in disgust.

grounded_facts: After the verdict, Longfellow is lifted and carried out by jubilant farmers and supporters.
memories.memory_text: I tried to reach Longfellow after the verdict, but the jubilant crowd lifted him onto their shoulders and carried him away, and I couldn't get through no matter how hard I tried.

grounded_facts: Babe is unable to reach Longfellow and is left alone in the courtroom after the crowd departs.
memories.memory_text: I tried to reach Longfellow, but the crowd was too thick and I couldn't get through — I jumped on a chair, I called out, but they carried him away and left me behind, all alone in the empty courtroom.

grounded_facts: Longfellow breaks away from the crowd, returns to the courtroom, and reunites with Babe.
memories.memory_text: I saw Longfellow break away from the crowd and come back to me in the courtroom.

grounded_facts: Longfellow returns to the courtroom and sweeps Babe into his arms, leading to a passionate embrace.
memories.memory_text: I felt him sweep me into his arms, and I kissed him over and over, finally feeling him kiss me back passionately.

Longfellow is informed that he has inherited approximately $20 million from his late uncle Martin W. Semple.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Cedar that my late uncle Martin W. Semple left me his entire fortune, which came to about $20 million after taxes.

grounded_facts: Longfellow responds to the news of his inheritance with mild surprise and states he does not need the money.
memories.memory_text: When I heard about the $20 million, I said it was quite a lot and admitted I didn't need it, wondering why my uncle left it to me.

grounded_facts: Cedar explains that Cobb served as a buffer for Longfellow's uncle, managing public and social access.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Cedar that Cobb had served as a buffer for my uncle, managing who could get to him socially, though I wasn't quite sure what that meant at the time.

grounded_facts: Longfellow composes and recites a limerick about Cobb losing his job after Semple's death, unintentionally causing discomfort.
memories.memory_text: I composed and recited a limerick about Cobb losing his job after Semple's death, not realizing it would make anyone uncomfortable.

grounded_facts: Mrs. Meredith comments on Longfellow's 'foolish notions' about saving a lady in distress, exposing his romantic idealism.
memories.memory_text: I was told that Mrs. Meredith commented on my foolish notions about saving a lady in distress, which made me realize how others see my ideals.

grounded_facts: A gathering during which Cedar and Cobb inform Longfellow of his inheritance and travel plans.
memories.memory_text: I was having lunch with Cedar and Cobb when they told me about my inheritance and that we'd be leaving for New York—I remember Cobb saying we'd meet at the train at four o'clock.

grounded_facts: After initial hesitation, Longfellow accepts the need to pack and travel to New York.
memories.memory_text: I realized we didn't have any suitcases, but I accepted that I needed to pack and meet the others at the train at four o'clock.

grounded_facts: Longfellow is informed that he is about to become one of the richest men in the country and must travel to New York.
memories.memory_text: I was told I'm about to become one of the richest men in the country and must travel to New York, and I remember hearing congratulations, Mr. Deeds, we'll see you later.

grounded_facts: A public town event held at the station to bid farewell to Longfellow Deeds, featuring a band, singing, and a large painted sign.
memories.memory_text: I remember the whole town showing up at the station for what they thought was my farewell, with the band playing and everyone singing, and that big, awkward sign painted just for me.

grounded_facts: Longfellow, who was previously missing and believed to have changed his mind, is discovered playing tuba in the town band during the farewell ceremony.
memories.memory_text: I was right there in the band, playing my tuba like always, and I could see Cobb spot me and quickly tell Cedar — I hadn't run off after all.

grounded_facts: A public send-off event at the station as Longfellow departs by train, attended by friends and well-wishers.
memories.memory_text: I stood on the observation platform of the train, seeing the crowd yell their farewells, baskets of fruit being handed up, and the band playing 'Auld Lang Syne' as I prepared to leave.

grounded_facts: Longfellow leaves the station aboard a moving train, marking the end of his physical presence in the current setting.
memories.memory_text: I smiled wanly and waved as the train began pulling out, knowing I was leaving the station and the town behind.

grounded_facts: Longfellow calls out personal goodbyes to specific people in the crowd before reflecting on his friendships.
memories.memory_text: I called out, 'Goodbye, Mrs. Meredith! Goodbye, Jim! Bye, Buddy! Goodbye, everybody!'—making sure to say personal goodbyes before reflecting on the friendships I made.

grounded_facts: Cobb looks up at Longfellow and is visibly moved by the farewell scene.
memories.memory_text: I noticed Cobb looking up at me, clearly moved by the scene, his expression showing how much the moment meant to him.

grounded_facts: Cobb offers Longfellow a drink in a social gesture.
memories.memory_text: Cobb offered me a drink, so I remember being told to have one, but I wasn't in the mood.

grounded_facts: Cedar offers Longfellow a cigar, continuing the attempt at social ease.
memories.memory_text: Cedar offered me a cigar, trying to make things friendly, so I heard him suggest we relax a bit.

grounded_facts: Longfellow refuses Cobb's offer of a drink and Cedar's offer of a cigar, showing distraction and disengagement from the social overtures.
memories.memory_text: I said no to both the drink and the cigar because I was distracted and didn't feel like engaging in small talk or indulgences.

grounded_facts: A private meeting aboard a train where Longfellow is informed about or discusses his inheritance, attended by Cobb and Cedar.
memories.memory_text: I was on the train with Cobb and Cedar, and they told me about the inheritance while I was lost in thought, trying to figure out how to replace a tuba player back home.

grounded_facts: Cedar attempts to alleviate Longfellow's perceived anxiety about managing the inheritance.
Cedar attempts to calm Longfellow by minimizing the burden of the inheritance and offering full management of affairs.
memories.memory_text: I remember Cedar telling me not to worry about the inheritance, saying I'd have plenty of help and to leave everything to him.

grounded_facts: Longfellow discloses that his real preoccupation is not the inheritance, but the replacement of a tuba player in a band, indicating detachment or absurdity.
memories.memory_text: I found myself wondering where they were going to get another tuba player for the band.

grounded_facts: Longfellow confirms and authorizes a telegram to Jim Mason instructing not to fire Arthur, whom he remembers as the last baby his father delivered.
memories.memory_text: I remember confirming the telegram to Jim Mason not to fire Arthur because he was the last baby my father ever delivered.

grounded_facts: Longfellow expresses suspicion about Cedar's offer to manage his affairs for free, indicating he will think further about granting Power of Attorney after recalling a similar unsolicited offer from someone named Winslow.
memories.memory_text: I told Cedar I’d give the Power of Attorney matter a lot of thought because a fellow named Winslow had also wanted to handle my affairs for nothing, and it puzzled me why people would work for free—it didn’t seem natural—so I decided I’d better think it over more.

grounded_facts: Cedar tries to prevent Hallor from seeing Longfellow directly, insisting he deal through him instead, revealing his desire to control information flow.
memories.memory_text: I saw Cedar try to block Hallor from coming in, telling someone not to let him in and insisting he deal through him instead.

grounded_facts: Hallor resists being pushed aside by Cedar, asserting his right to speak directly to Longfellow on behalf of his client.
memories.memory_text: I witnessed Hallor push back against Cedar when he tried to shut him out, saying he was tired of being pushed around no matter how important Cedar thought he was.

grounded_facts: Longfellow discovers that his uncle had a common-law wife, Mrs. Semple, and a child, both of whom have a legal claim on the estate.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Hallor that my uncle had a common-law wife, Mrs. Semple, and that she and a child—my uncle's child—have a legal claim on the estate.

grounded_facts: Upon learning of Mrs. Semple and her child, Longfellow immediately decides she should be taken care of and that she should have all the money if she was his uncle's wife.
memories.memory_text: I learned that Mrs. Semple was my uncle's common-law wife and that there's a child, and I immediately felt she should be taken care of—if she was his wife, she should have all the money and I don't want a penny of it.

grounded_facts: Longfellow asks Cobb to accompany him to the opera board meeting because he feels uncomfortable among strangers.
memories.memory_text: I asked Cobb to come with me to the opera board meeting because I feel uncomfortable around strangers and I’d feel better having him there.

grounded_facts: A meeting in Longfellow's bedroom where he is being fitted for a suit, during which business matters and legal claims are discussed in the presence of Cedar, Cobb, and tailors.
memories.memory_text: I remember standing in my bedroom while tailors fitted me for a suit, and during that time, Cedar, Cobb, and others were present as we discussed business matters and legal claims, including a man named Hallor who came to see me about Mrs. Semple’s claim on my uncle’s estate.

grounded_facts: Cobb responds to Longfellow's question about why opera people always meet in this location by drawing an analogy to mice going where there's cheese, implying the place naturally attracts them.
memories.memory_text: I asked Cobb if opera people always met here, and he said yes, then explained it by asking me why mice go where there's cheese, as if the answer was obvious.

grounded_facts: A formal meeting of board members convened to obtain financial commitment from Longfellow for a $180,000 amount.
memories.memory_text: I remember the board members sitting around a long table waiting for me, clearly expecting to get my financial commitment for $180,000.

grounded_facts: Douglas explains to Longfellow that as Chairman, he presides over meetings.
memories.memory_text: I was told that as Chairman, I preside over the meetings.

memories.memory_text: I remember the Treasurer reporting an $180,000 deficit for the year, and the silence that followed was broken only by a siren growing louder outside.

grounded_facts: A formal gathering of the opera company's Board of Directors to conduct organizational business, including electing a new Chairman and reviewing reports.
memories.memory_text: I attended a formal meeting of the opera company's Board of Directors where I was told the first order of business was electing a new Chairman, and later I learned they were also reviewing reports like the Treasurer's, even though I didn't fully understand what the Chairman was supposed to do at first.

grounded_facts: Upon learning of the financial loss, Longfellow declares he will not contribute his money without scrutiny and decides to leave the board.
memories.memory_text: I told the board I couldn't afford to put my money into anything without looking into it first, especially if it's losing $180,000—there must be something wrong, and I expect to do a lot of good with that money.

grounded_facts: Longfellow Deeds is nominated and unanimously elected as the new Chairman of the Board in a sentimental gesture honoring his late uncle.
memories.memory_text: I was nominated and unanimously elected as the new Chairman of the Board in a sentimental gesture honoring my late uncle, Mr. Semple, but when I found out the opera was losing $180,000 and that I'd be expected to cover it, I decided I couldn't support it without looking into what was wrong first, so I resigned and walked out.

grounded_facts: Longfellow questions the sustainability and logic of running an unprofitable opera, implying mismanagement.
memories.memory_text: I questioned why we were losing so much money running the opera, wondering if we were giving the wrong kind of shows or charging too much, and I made it clear that I couldn't afford to fund something that kept losing $180,000 without looking into it first.

grounded_facts: Cobb sarcastically suggests the directors use smelling salts, ridiculing their stunned reaction.
memories.memory_text: I heard Cobb mock the directors by suggesting they use smelling salts, making fun of how stunned they were when I announced I was leaving.

grounded_facts: Longfellow decides not to invest $180,000 in an opera project, dismissing the request as absurd.
memories.memory_text: I turned down the opera people when they asked for $180,000—I thought it was absurd and naturally said no.

grounded_facts: Longfellow rejects wearing a tailcoat, calling it a 'monkey suit' and expressing discomfort with formal dress.
memories.memory_text: I refused to wear that tailcoat Walter brought in because I called it a monkey suit and said I'd never worn one in my life, and I didn't want anyone touching my pants either.

grounded_facts: A formal meeting in Longfellow's bedroom where legal and financial matters are discussed, culminating in Hallor's dismissal.
memories.memory_text: I had a meeting in my bedroom where I dismissed Hallor after deciding he wasn't trustworthy, telling him to leave through the front door.

Longfellow accuses Hallor of being a crook and forcibly ejects him after rejecting his legal proposal regarding Mrs. Semple's claim.
memories.memory_text: I told Hallor there wasn't any wife and no letters, and I called him a crook because I believed he was trying to cheat me, then I made sure he left — I wasn't going to let him stay after rejecting his proposal about Mrs. Semple's claim.

grounded_facts: Cobb acknowledges Longfellow's integrity by saying 'Lamb bites wolf,' signaling a shift in allegiance.
memories.memory_text: I heard Cobb say to me, 'Lamb bites wolf,' and I knew he was finally acknowledging that I wasn't going to play along with the corruption—he was choosing to stand with me.

grounded_facts: Cedar adopts a forced smile and praises Longfellow's actions, attempting to maintain favor.
memories.memory_text: I saw Cedar put on a forced smile and act like he was on my side, but I wasn't convinced he had honest intentions.

grounded_facts: Longfellow instructs Cedar to organize the financial books so he can review them, asserting control over his estate management.
memories.memory_text: I told Cedar he's not my attorney yet and made him get the financial books ready so I can review them myself.

grounded_facts: Cobb offers Longfellow women for entertainment, which Longfellow declines, expressing discomfort with the proposition.
memories.memory_text: I declined Cobb's offer of women for entertainment when he told me to name my poison, saying I'd pass for now.

grounded_facts: Longfellow expresses disgust at Cobb's commodification of women, comparing it to cattle.
memories.memory_text: I expressed my disgust to the valet, saying Cobb talks about women as if they were cattle.

grounded_facts: Longfellow inquires about his uncle's rumored behavior and learns that he once hosted up to twenty women simultaneously.
memories.memory_text: I asked the valet about my uncle's past and learned he once had as many as twenty women in the house at the same time.

grounded_facts: Longfellow asks the bodyguards to retrieve a trunk from a room, which they agree to do, leading to the opportunity for him to lock them in.
memories.memory_text: I asked the bodyguards to get my trunk from the room before we went out, and they agreed to do it for me.

grounded_facts: Longfellow takes the opportunity to lock his bodyguards in a closet after they enter it to retrieve his trunk, thereby escaping their supervision.

memories.memory_text: I came out of the house and looked toward the horizon, feeling happy as a light drizzle filled the air around me.

memories.memory_text: I lifted her head and saw her eyes open, looking up at me with feigned bewilderment.

memories.memory_text: I asked her if I could help and offered her my house, wanting her to feel welcome and safe.

grounded_facts: Longfellow expresses concern by asking Babe what caused her fainting.
memories.memory_text: I asked her what happened, worried about why she had collapsed.

memories.memory_text: She told me she had been looking for a job all day and found one starting tomorrow.

memories.memory_text: I watched as she insisted she was fine, thanked me, and walked away despite my concern.

memories.memory_text: I saw a girl stagger out of the shadows and collapse near a tree in front of my house, so I rushed over and lifted her head, thinking she had fainted, and later she seemed to weaken again and fell against the fence.

grounded_facts: After walking a few steps, Babe pretends to weaken again and falls against the iron fence, prompting Longfellow to rush to her aid.
memories.memory_text: I saw Babe take a few steps and then feign weakness again, falling against the iron fence and clutching it, so I rushed to her assistance.

grounded_facts: Seeing Babe's renewed distress, Longfellow looks around and calls for a taxi to assist her.
memories.memory_text: Seeing Babe in distress again, I looked around and called out, 'Hey, taxi!' to get help for her.

grounded_facts: A group of established poets, including Brookfield and Henaberry, gather at a round table in Tullio's restaurant for drinks and conversation.
memories.memory_text: I saw Brookfield and a group of poets gathered at a big round table in Tullio's, the one that looked like a poodle, and I pointed him out to Babe.

grounded_facts: Brookfield rises to personally invite Longfellow to join the poets' table, prompted by the waiter's introduction.
memories.memory_text: I noticed the waiter whisper to Brookfield about me wanting to meet him, and then I saw Brookfield rise from the table, saying he'd come get me.

grounded_facts: Longfellow recognizes that the poets are making fun of him, leading to emotional hurt and a decision to leave.
memories.memory_text: I realized they invited me here just to make fun of me, and it hurt — I could see it in their laughter, and I knew I didn't belong. I told them it's easy to mock someone when you don't care how much you hurt them, and I decided we'd be leaving.

grounded_facts: Longfellow directly calls out the poets for mocking him and expresses disappointment in their lack of kindness.
memories.memory_text: I called out Mr. Brookfield directly, telling him I was disappointed in him despite liking his poems, and I said that no one in Mandrake Falls would treat a visitor that way. I even said I’d bump their heads together if Babe weren’t here with me.

grounded_facts: After deciding to leave, Longfellow returns to deliver two quick punches to Brookfield and Henaberry in retaliation for their mockery.
memories.memory_text: I decided to leave after their mockery, but then I came back and punched Brookfield with my left fist and caught Henaberry on the jaw with my right.

grounded_facts: Morrow shouts 'Eureka!' and rises to follow Longfellow, showing respect for his integrity and courage.
Morrow, who remained silent during the mockery, expresses sudden admiration for Longfellow by exclaiming 'Eureka!' as he rises to follow him.
memories.memory_text: I heard Morrow shout 'Eureka!' as he got up to follow me, showing his respect after staying silent during the others' mockery.

grounded_facts: In a drunken but self-aware gesture, Morrow invites Longfellow to punch him in the chin as a form of playful penance.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Morrow, in the midst of his drunkenness, to hit him right on the chin—just sock it hard—as if it were some kind of joke or penance he was asking for.

grounded_facts: Morrow admits he has behaved like a 'skunk' and offers to symbolically punish himself by eating postcards at a newsstand.
memories.memory_text: I saw Morrow admit he’d been a skunk and offer to eat a pack of postcards raw at a newsstand, right there in front of me, as a way to make up for how he’d acted.

grounded_facts: As Morrow becomes increasingly unsteady, Longfellow repeatedly grabs his collar to prevent him from falling over.
memories.memory_text: I remember grabbing Morrow’s collar several times to keep him from falling over as he swayed while talking, his drunkenness making him unsteady on his feet.

grounded_facts: Morrow exaggerates the scope of the night out by claiming they will visit global landmarks like the Leaning Tower of Pisa and Mount Everest in a single evening.
memories.memory_text: I was told that night we’d lean against the Leaning Tower of Pisa and climb Mount Everest, and though he spoke with wild excitement, I took it as part of his playful exaggeration rather than a literal plan.

grounded_facts: After apologizing for his earlier behavior, Morrow enthusiastically invites Longfellow and Babe to join him on a wild night of drinking and exploration across New York City.
memories.memory_text: I remember Morrow apologizing for his earlier behavior and then enthusiastically inviting me and Babe to join him on a wild night of drinking and adventure across New York City, promising to show us sights we'd never seen before and take us on a binge that would be unforgettable.

grounded_facts: A proposed evening of heavy drinking and social adventuring through New York City, led by Morrow, intended to introduce Longfellow and Babe to eccentric characters and surreal experiences.
memories.memory_text: I remember Morrow telling me about a wild night he wanted to take me and Babe on through New York City, full of eccentric people and surreal adventures, saying it would be a binge to remember and that he’d show me sights leaping from sphinx to sphinx like something out of a dream.

grounded_facts: Mac reads Babe's article about Longfellow Deeds aloud in his office, reacting with excitement to its content and impact.
memories.memory_text: I remember Mac reading Babe's article aloud in his office, and I could see how excited he was by the story's content.

grounded_facts: Mac praises Babe for creating the memorable nickname 'Cinderella Man' for Longfellow Deeds, recognizing its sensational impact.
Mac enthusiastically compliments Babe on the quality and sensationalism of her story about Deeds.
memories.memory_text: I was told that Mac praised Babe for coming up with the nickname 'Cinderella Man' and called her a genius, saying it was sensational and would stick with me forever.

grounded_facts: Babe discloses that she is posing as Mary Dawson, a stenographer, and has moved into Mabel Dawson's apartment to maintain her cover.
memories.memory_text: I was told that Babe is actually Mary Dawson, a stenographer, and that she moved into Mabel Dawson's apartment to keep up her cover.

grounded_facts: Mac instructs Babe to stay close to Deeds and produce daily exclusive stories to dominate the competition.
memories.memory_text: I witnessed Mac instructing Babe to stay close to me and write daily exclusive stories so their paper could dominate the competition.

grounded_facts: When Mac moves toward her as if to kiss her, Babe sidesteps and reminds him their deal is strictly professional.
memories.memory_text: When Mac moved toward me as if to kiss me, I sidestepped and reminded him our deal was strictly professional — a month's vacation with pay.

grounded_facts: Longfellow remembers Miss Dawson, a woman he tried to help, and expresses regret for not taking her home.
memories.memory_text: I remember Miss Dawson—she was a lady in distress with a lot of pride, and I regret that I don't recall taking her home last night. I should call her and apologize.

grounded_facts: Longfellow regains consciousness after a night of heavy drinking, unable to recall key events, including losing his clothes and being brought home by police.
memories.memory_text: I woke up confused this morning, barely remembering anything from last night. Walter was shaking me, and it took a moment to regain my bearings—I could feel that something had happened, but the details were slipping away.

grounded_facts: Walter tells Longfellow he returned home naked except for shorts, carried by police after public outbursts.
