memories.memory_text: I was told I came home last night without any clothes, just in my shorts, and that the police carried me after I was shouting in the streets about 'back to nature'.

grounded_facts: Longfellow reads a telegram revealing that Arthur, a shipping clerk, demands a raise or will quit his job.
memories.memory_text: I read a telegram that arrived for me, and I learned Arthur, the shipping clerk at the Tallow Works, is demanding a $2 raise or he'll quit his job.

grounded_facts: A private, chaotic morning session in Longfellow's bedroom where he confronts the consequences of his drunken night, receives urgent messages, and is confronted by Cobb about public image.
memories.memory_text: I asked Walter if Miss Dawson had called, and when he said no, I insisted on finding the number I’d written down. As I sat up, I saw the telegram and then Cobb burst in with a newspaper—his face was urgent, and when I saw the paper, my mood darkened.

grounded_facts: Cobb urgently demands Longfellow stop talking to people to prevent media exploitation.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Cobb that I need to keep my trap shut and not talk to anybody because the newshounds are out gunning for me, and if I keep talking, he can't protect me from the press.

grounded_facts: Under pressure from Cobb, Longfellow agrees to remain silent to prevent further media exploitation.
memories.memory_text: I agreed to remain silent from now on because Cobb pressured me to stop speaking publicly, and I said, 'Yes, I guess I'll have to,' knowing it was the only way to prevent further media exploitation.

grounded_facts: Cobb arrives urgently, showing Longfellow newspaper reports of his bizarre behavior and the 'Cinderella Man' nickname, demanding he stop speaking to the press.
memories.memory_text: Cobb came to me urgently, showing me newspaper stories that mocked my behavior and called me the 'Cinderella Man,' and he demanded I stop speaking to the press to keep the situation from getting worse.

grounded_facts: Miss Dawson contacts Longfellow by phone, marking a personal reconnection after his failed attempt to help her.
memories.memory_text: I remember when Miss Dawson called me—I asked, 'Who? Miss Dawson?' and then told them to give me the phone right away because she's the only one I'm going to talk to from now on.

grounded_facts: Longfellow thanks Babe for showing him around New York, indicating appreciation for the experience.
memories.memory_text: I thanked Babe for showing me around New York because I really appreciated him taking the time to do that.

grounded_facts: Longfellow expresses enthusiasm about the Aquarium, calling it 'swell' and suggesting he would visit daily if he lived in New York.
memories.memory_text: I told Babe the Aquarium was swell and said I'd go there every day if I lived in New York.

grounded_facts: Babe expresses that he would like to visit the Aquarium more often but is limited by his job responsibilities.
memories.memory_text: I heard Babe say he'd like to visit the Aquarium more often, but he has a job to think of, so he can't.

grounded_facts: Longfellow diverts the conversation by telling Babe she looks pretty tonight, avoiding her question about the opera board's decision.
memories.memory_text: I told Babe she looked pretty tonight to shift the conversation away from the opera board's decision.

grounded_facts: Longfellow reports that the opera board rejected his proposal to lower prices, cut expenses, and broadcast performances, calling him crazy and accusing him of wanting to run it like a grocery store.
memories.memory_text: I remember that Longfellow reports that the opera board rejected his proposal to lower prices, cut expenses, and broadcast performances, calling him crazy and accusing him of wanting to run it like a grocery store.

grounded_facts: Longfellow leans in and asks Babe if she always wears her hair that way, indicating romantic interest and physical closeness.
memories.memory_text: I leaned in and asked Babe if she always wears her hair that way, feeling drawn to her and wanting to get closer.

grounded_facts: Babe becomes aware that the public is ridiculing Longfellow with the nickname 'Cinderella Man' through overhearing passing girls and Longfellow's subsequent reaction.
memories.memory_text: I overheard some girls passing by, laughing and calling me 'Cinderella Man' like it was some big joke, and one of them said she'd like to get her hooks into the guy writing about me, which let me know how people were really talking behind my back.

grounded_facts: After the girls mock him, Longfellow mutters that he would knock their heads together if they were men, showing repressed anger and gendered response to insult.
memories.memory_text: After those girls mocked me, I muttered that if they were men, I'd knock their heads together, because I was so furious but had to hold myself back.

grounded_facts: Longfellow appreciates that Babe considers his feelings about the negative press, reinforcing emotional connection.
memories.memory_text: I really appreciated that Babe thought about how I'd feel reading those stories, and I told her that's what I like about her—she actually cares about a man's feelings.

grounded_facts: An intimate nighttime conversation between Babe and Longfellow while riding on top of a bus, covering personal feelings, professional challenges, and public perception.

grounded_facts: Longfellow expresses violent frustration toward the journalist writing negative stories, saying he’d like to punch him in the nose.
memories.memory_text: I told Babe I'd like to go down to the newspaper and punch the fellow in the nose who's writing those nasty stories about me, because it made me so angry to think people were believing that garbage.

grounded_facts: To relieve tension, Babe shifts focus from the humiliating topic and suggests walking the rest of the way, prompting both characters to leave the bus.
Babe and Longfellow agree to get off the bus and walk the remainder of their journey, marking a joint decision to continue their time together in a more private setting.
memories.memory_text: I remember Babe suggesting we walk the rest of the way to ease the tension, and I agreed—she got up from her seat and I followed, happy to keep spending time with her away from the bus.

grounded_facts: Babe encourages Longfellow to move toward Grant's Tomb, unaware of his emotional state.
memories.memory_text: I stood there feeling overwhelmed, and Babe urged me to go toward Grant's Tomb, asking if I wanted to see it, though I didn't respond.

grounded_facts: A group taxi tour stops at Grant's Tomb, where passengers observe the monument and engage in reflective conversation.
memories.memory_text: I was on a group taxi tour that stopped at Grant's Tomb, where we all got out to see the monument and the others shared their thoughts about it.

grounded_facts: Babe asks Longfellow what he sees at Grant's Tomb, prompting his emotional and poetic response.
memories.memory_text: Babe asked me what I saw at Grant's Tomb, prompting me to share my thoughts.

grounded_facts: Longfellow articulates an idealized, emotional vision of American history and possibility inspired by Grant's Tomb, revealing his deep patriotic sentiment and personal hope.
memories.memory_text: I shared an emotional vision of America's promise, seeing Grant as a farm boy turned great soldier and president, and believing such things can only happen in a country like America.

grounded_facts: Longfellow's heartfelt speech affects Babe, who is fascinated and unable to laugh despite her initial impulse.
memories.memory_text: I spoke from the heart, and I could see Babe watching me, fascinated—she started out wanting to laugh, but I could tell she couldn't, not anymore.

grounded_facts: A private nighttime conversation between Longfellow and Babe on the roof of a tall building overlooking Times Square, involving personal reflections and emotional tension.
memories.memory_text: I had a private conversation with Babe on the roof of a tall building overlooking Times Square, where we shared personal thoughts and I felt some emotional tension between us.

grounded_facts: After Longfellow's attempt to spit on Times Square fails and the wind blows it back on him, Babe laughs and wipes it off his coat with a handkerchief.
memories.memory_text: I tried to spit on Times Square, but the wind blew it back on me, and Babe laughed and wiped it off my coat with her handkerchief.

grounded_facts: Babe displays a guilty expression when questioned about whether she believes the negative stories about Longfellow.
memories.memory_text: When I asked Babe if she believed all that stuff about me, I noticed she looked guilty, like she might have believed some of it.

grounded_facts: Longfellow acknowledges that negative articles about him will continue but claims he is no longer concerned.
memories.memory_text: I told Babe I'm not worrying anymore about the articles—they'll keep writing them until they get tired, and that's fine with me.

grounded_facts: Longfellow expresses confusion and sadness about why people enjoy hurting each other instead of trying to like one another.
memories.memory_text: I remember asking Babe why people seem to get so much pleasure out of hurting each other instead of trying to like one another—I just couldn't understand it.

grounded_facts: Longfellow nervously asks if Babe is engaged, signaling romantic interest.
memories.memory_text: I nervously asked Babe if she was engaged, hoping to find out if she might be romantically available.

grounded_facts: Babe asks why Longfellow doesn't go out with girls, prompting him to reflect on his isolation.
memories.memory_text: I remember Babe asking me why I don’t go out with girls, and whether I didn’t like the society girls I’ve met since coming here—she was the one who brought it up, curious about my life.

grounded_facts: Longfellow reflects on the emptiness of elite social life, comparing it to grand palaces without noblemen, indicating his alienation from the environment.
memories.memory_text: I remember reflecting to Babe how, after leaving her one night, I walked and looked at the city’s tall buildings and thought about what Thoreau said—that they built grand palaces but forgot to create the noblemen to live in them, and how that made me feel how empty this elite world really is.

grounded_facts: Babe discloses that she comes from a small town similar to Mandrake Falls, creating a sense of shared identity with Longfellow.
memories.memory_text: I remember Babe telling me she's from a small town too, probably as small as Mandrake Falls, which made me feel a sudden sense of connection.

grounded_facts: Babe tells Longfellow that he reminds her of her father, establishing deep emotional resonance.
Babe recalls her childhood and her father, revealing emotional depth and drawing a parallel between him and Longfellow.
memories.memory_text: I recall Babe saying her father was a lot like me—he talked like I do, and she even kissed him sometimes while they fished together, which she shared with such warmth that it moved me.

grounded_facts: Babe plays and sings 'Swanee River' using sticks on a bench, sharing a personal talent tied to her father's teaching.
memories.memory_text: I watched Babe pick up two sticks and drum on the bench while singing 'Swanee River,' sharing a talent her father had taught her.

grounded_facts: After Babe sings, Longfellow pretends disappointment, then offers to sing 'Humoresque' with her.
memories.memory_text: After she finished, I made a show of being disappointed, then I told her, 'Sure. Look! You sing it over again, and I'll do "Humoresque" with you.'

grounded_facts: An intimate conversation between Babe and Longfellow while hidden in bushes, marked by emotional openness and mutual discovery.
memories.memory_text: I remember that quiet moment with Babe, hidden in the bushes, when we opened up to each other—she reminded me of what I’d said about her being a lady in distress, and I asked if she was engaged. When she smiled and said no, I felt something shift. She asked why I don’t go out with girls, and I admitted I haven’t met anyone here I really like—everyone seems to have the St. Vitus Dance, I said, except her. I told her people here work so hard at living they forget how to live, and how, after leaving her the night before, I walked past the tall buildings and thought about Thoreau—how they built grand palaces but forgot to make noblemen to fill them. Then she surprised me by saying she was from a small town too, and shared a sweet memory about fishing with her father, who sounded a lot like me. Later, when she started drumming and offered to sing 'Swanee River,' I joined in, suggesting we do 'Humoresque' together, and we made music in counterpoint, just the two of us.

grounded_facts: Longfellow joins Babe musically by singing 'Humoresque' in harmony with her performance, creating a shared artistic moment.
memories.memory_text: I joined Babe by singing 'Humoresque' in counterpoint to her drumming, creating a joyful moment of harmony between us.

grounded_facts: Longfellow and Babe sing together in the park, drawing brief attention from a passing policeman and being covertly observed by Bob and Frank.
memories.memory_text: I sang with Babe in the park, and we were having such a grand time that we both laughed joyously by the end.

grounded_facts: Longfellow runs to the fire engine, excitedly hops aboard, and identifies himself as a fire volunteer from Mandrake Falls.
memories.memory_text: I heard the siren getting louder, so I jumped up and ran to the fire engine, excitedly hopping aboard—I remembered to tell them I'm a fire volunteer from Mandrake Falls.

grounded_facts: Longfellow salutes and introduces himself as Captain Deeds, a fire volunteer from Mandrake Falls, to the firefighter.
memories.memory_text: I saluted and introduced myself as Captain Deeds, a fire volunteer from Mandrake Falls, and I could see the firefighter greet me with a smile, calling me 'Cap' and welcoming me to the crew.

grounded_facts: Seeing Longfellow's sudden action, Bob and Frank decide the evening is not wasted and begin actively filming again.
memories.memory_text: I saw the fire engine coming and got excited, jumping up and running toward the street, and I noticed Bob and Frank suddenly grabbing their cameras and running after me, like they’d just realized the night wasn’t a waste after all.

grounded_facts: Longfellow Deeds calls Babe, and she takes the phone from Mabel upon hearing his nickname.
memories.memory_text: I was told that the 'Cinderella Man' was on the phone, and I took it right away to speak with him.

grounded_facts: Longfellow is unable to sleep and expresses a desire to talk to someone on the phone.
Longfellow initiates a phone call due to insomnia and emotional need for conversation.
memories.memory_text: I couldn't sleep, so I picked up the phone because I really wanted to talk to someone and get some relief from how I was feeling.

grounded_facts: Longfellow tells Babe that the poem he is writing is about her, using creative expression to communicate emotions.
memories.memory_text: I told Babe the poem I'm writing is about her, because I wanted to share how I feel in a way that feels easier for me.

grounded_facts: Longfellow thanks Babe for going out with him and expresses deep appreciation, indicating she compensates for past disappointing relationships.
Longfellow thanks Babe for going out with him and expresses how much she means to him compared to past relationships.
memories.memory_text: I thanked Babe for going out with me and told her how much she means to me, especially compared to past relationships, because I find it hard to say these things out loud.

grounded_facts: Longfellow discloses he has been writing a poem about Babe, using poetry as a medium for expressing feelings he finds hard to say directly.
memories.memory_text: I told Babe I've been working on a poem since I got home, and I explained that sometimes it's hard for me to say things out loud, so I write them instead.

grounded_facts: Babe responds emotionally to the news of the poem and expresses interest in reading it in the future.
Babe expresses her desire to read the poem Longfellow is writing about her.
memories.memory_text: I remember Babe telling me she'd like to read my poem someday, and the way she said it made me feel she really cared about what I was writing for her.

grounded_facts: Longfellow asks Babe when they will meet again and expresses enthusiasm upon hearing it will be soon.
Longfellow asks Babe if he will see her soon and reacts positively to her response.
memories.memory_text: I asked Babe if I’d see her soon, and when she said yes, I couldn’t help but say how swell it was—my heart just lit up.

grounded_facts: A telephone conversation between Longfellow and Babe, occurring in Longfellow's bedroom, where emotional intimacy is deepened.
memories.memory_text: I called Babe from my bedroom and we talked warmly, and after we said good night, I hung up and just lay there feeling deeply moved by how close we’ve become.

grounded_facts: After hanging up, Longfellow lies back, emotionally affected and absorbed by the connection with Babe.
memories.memory_text: After I hung up, I lay back and just let the feeling of being close to Babe wash over me—I was completely absorbed.

grounded_facts: Walter enters Longfellow's bedroom while he is playing the tuba and delivers a message about a phone call.
memories.memory_text: I was playing the tuba in bed when Walter came in and interrupted me.

grounded_facts: Longfellow ceases playing the tuba after being interrupted by Walter.
memories.memory_text: I stopped playing the tuba right after Walter walked into my room and disturbed me.

grounded_facts: Madame Pomponi calls to confirm arrangements for an upcoming reception.
memories.memory_text: I was told that Madame Pomponi called to confirm the reception arrangements.

grounded_facts: Longfellow angrily orders Walter to leave after being interrupted.
memories.memory_text: I angrily told Walter to get out after he interrupted my tuba practice.

grounded_facts: After expelling Walter, Longfellow jumps up and chases him down the grand staircase.
memories.memory_text: I jumped up and chased Walter down the grand staircase after expelling him from the room.

grounded_facts: While chasing Walter, Longfellow suddenly stops at the top of the stairs, struck by a new thought.
memories.memory_text: I suddenly stopped at the top of the stairs, struck by a new thought while chasing Walter.

grounded_facts: Longfellow orders Walter to make a sound to test the echo, escalating from a timid hoot to louder attempts.
memories.memory_text: I told Walter to make a sound to test the echo, and when he started too quietly, I called down for him to be louder.

grounded_facts: Longfellow commands the butler to join the echo test, which the butler eagerly accepts.
memories.memory_text: I saw the butler come out in his bathrobe, and I told him to try the echo test—he asked if he really should, so I urged him to speak louder.

grounded_facts: Longfellow points to and instructs another servant to participate in the echo test.
memories.memory_text: I pointed to another man-servant who had just appeared and told him to join in and try the echo test too.

grounded_facts: An informal, spontaneous gathering on the grand staircase where Longfellow leads household members in testing and enjoying the echo effect through vocalizations.
memories.memory_text: I gathered everyone on the staircase, including the butler who came out in his bathrobe, and I called out 'All together!' to make a group sound and enjoy the echo.

grounded_facts: Longfellow initiates an impromptu test of the staircase's acoustics by shouting and observing the echo, confirming its presence.
memories.memory_text: I shouted from the top of the staircase to test the acoustics, and when I heard the echo bounce back, I knew it was working.

grounded_facts: Under Longfellow's direction, multiple servants join in producing sounds to create a collective auditory effect with echoes.
memories.memory_text: I saw the butler come out in his bathrobe, and I made sure he joined in with the others, helping me build that wave of sound echoing down the stairs.

grounded_facts: Longfellow orchestrates a synchronized round of vocalizations from the entire group.
memories.memory_text: I conducted the whole group, raising my hand and calling out 'All together!' to start the synchronized round of voices.

grounded_facts: Longfellow concludes the echo exercise with a dramatic statement and withdraws to his bedroom.
memories.memory_text: I concluded the echo exercise with a dramatic statement, telling them, 'Let that be a lesson to you,' and then I spun on my heel and returned to my bedroom.

grounded_facts: After Longfellow leaves, the butler asserts authority by ordering the others to return to their rooms.
After Longfellow departs, the butler assumes control and orders the other servants to return to their rooms.
memories.memory_text: After I left, I saw the butler step forward and order the others to go back to their rooms.

grounded_facts: Babe cancels her date with Longfellow, indicating she is not going out tonight.
memories.memory_text: I was told the date was off because Babe’s friend was having a party at his house, so she wasn’t going out tonight.

grounded_facts: Longfellow Deeds arrives at the apartment looking for Mary Dawson, initiating a shift in the scene’s dynamics.
memories.memory_text: I arrived at the apartment and asked if Mary Dawson was there, introducing myself as Longfellow Deeds.

grounded_facts: Mabel pretends that Babe is Mary Dawson and that she herself is Mary’s sister, creating a false identity framework.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Mabel that Babe is Mary Dawson and that she herself is Mary’s sister, setting up a false identity I accepted at the time.

grounded_facts: Longfellow's unexpected arrival at the apartment to see Babe, leading to an impromptu outing.
memories.memory_text: I went to Babe's apartment to see her, introduced myself as Longfellow Deeds, and said I threw the party guests out because they got on my nerves, leading to an impromptu outing.

grounded_facts: Longfellow reveals he threw out the guests at his party to come see Babe, showing his prioritization of her over social obligations.
memories.memory_text: I told Babe I threw out my party guests because I didn't want anything to stop me from seeing her, and I wasn't sorry about it either.

grounded_facts: Babe quickly proposes going for a walk with Longfellow, possibly to escape tension or shift focus.
memories.memory_text: I was with Babe when she suddenly asked me if I'd like to go for a walk, so I figured she wanted to change the mood.

grounded_facts: Longfellow compliments Babe on her appearance, expressing admiration.
memories.memory_text: I remember thinking to myself, 'Gosh, she looks better every time I see her,' and I really meant it.

grounded_facts: Mabel physically blocks Bob and Frank from leaving with their cameras, preventing them from photographing Longfellow and Babe.
Mabel blocks Bob and Frank from leaving to take photographs, asserting control over the situation.
memories.memory_text: I saw Mabel step in and block Bob and Frank from leaving with their cameras, stopping them from taking more photos of me and Babe.

grounded_facts: Longfellow reveals his decision to leave and return to Mandrake Falls in a day or so, indicating a shift in his personal trajectory.
memories.memory_text: I told Babe that I'm going home to Mandrake Falls in a day or so, because I don't fit in here and I haven't had time to figure out what to do with the money, so I decided to wait till I get back home to make sense of it all.

grounded_facts: Longfellow reveals his lifelong habit of talking to an imaginary girl while hiking, symbolizing his longing for connection and foreshadowing his feelings for Babe.
memories.memory_text: I told Babe about how I used to talk to an imaginary girl while hiking through the woods back home, because I've always wanted someone to talk to, and it made me feel less alone.

grounded_facts: Babe tells Longfellow goodbye with deep affection, affirming his reality and worth while releasing him.
memories.memory_text: I remember Babe saying goodbye to me with such deep affection, telling me not to let anyone hurt me and that I'm too real to be broken.

grounded_facts: Longfellow presents a completed poem addressed to Babe, expressing his deep love and emotional vulnerability.
memories.memory_text: I gave Babe my completed poem, telling her it was for her, and I felt completely exposed—my heart was in those words, confessing my love even if I couldn't say it out loud.

grounded_facts: Longfellow hands Babe the completed poem addressed to her, asking only that she read it, not respond immediately.
memories.memory_text: I handed her the poem and asked her to read it, but not to respond right away—I told her I’d wait until tomorrow to hear from her, because I needed time and so did she.

grounded_facts: After the passionate kiss, Babe realizes the hopelessness of the situation and begins to pull away from Longfellow.
memories.memory_text: I felt Babe start to pull away from my embrace, and I noticed she was weeping softly, but I didn't understand why she was sad.

grounded_facts: Babe reads the poem aloud, becomes overwhelmed with emotion, and ultimately embraces Longfellow.
memories.memory_text: I remember Babe reading my poem aloud, her voice trembling as she finished, and then she suddenly kissed me, throwing her arms around me — I held her close, feeling her weep before she gently pulled away.

grounded_facts: After the emotional exchange, Longfellow leaves in a burst of joy, stumbling down the street.
memories.memory_text: I let out a yelp of joy and leapt down the steps, tripping over a garbage pail and bumping into people as I zigzagged down the street, completely caught up in the moment.

grounded_facts: A walk taken by Longfellow and Babe around the block, beginning and ending at the front steps of Babe's home, during which significant emotional revelations occur.
memories.memory_text: I took a walk with Babe around the block, starting and ending at her home, and during that walk I felt a deep emotional connection when we embraced, and later I left with a burst of joy, tripping down the steps and running off into the street.

grounded_facts: Mac initially reacts with excitement to the news of the proposal, imagining a news story.
memories.memory_text: I got excited when I heard about the proposal and immediately thought of the headline: 'Cinderella Man Woos Mystery Girl! Who is the Mysterious Girl That...'

grounded_facts: Mac probes whether Babe has developed genuine feelings for the man she was assigned to investigate.
memories.memory_text: I asked Babe if she had actually fallen for that guy she was supposed to be investigating, because I needed to know if her feelings were real.

grounded_facts: Mac suggests reassigning Babe to avoid facing the emotional fallout.
memories.memory_text: I suggested reassigning Babe to a different job so she wouldn't have to face the emotional fallout, telling her she'd never have to see him again.

grounded_facts: Longfellow playfully slides down the bannister of the grand staircase upon exiting his room, indicating a lighthearted and energetic mood.
memories.memory_text: I emerged from my room feeling full of joy and couldn't resist sliding down the grand bannister just for the fun of it.

grounded_facts: A private dinner for two being prepared by Longfellow in anticipation of Babe's arrival.
memories.memory_text: I prepared a private dinner for two, expecting Babe to arrive soon.

grounded_facts: Longfellow asks if the butler obtained the pate de fois gras, which he refers to as 'goo' that tastes like soap, noting Babe likes it.
memories.memory_text: I asked the butler if he got the 'goo' that tastes like soap—pate de fois gras—and made sure there was plenty because I know Babe likes it.

grounded_facts: Longfellow commands the butler to replace the tall flower bowl with a smaller one so he can see across the table.
memories.memory_text: I told the butler the flowers were too high and asked him to replace them with a smaller bowl so I could see across the table.

grounded_facts: Longfellow sits at the table and silently mimics a conversation with Babe, testing the intimacy and positioning of the setup.
memories.memory_text: I sat at the table and leaned forward, silently mimicking a conversation with Babe, moving my lips as if we were really talking, just to test how the setup felt.

grounded_facts: Longfellow instructs the butler to sit at the table and adjust his posture to simulate Babe's presence during a rehearsal.
memories.memory_text: I instructed the butler to sit at the table and change his posture to simulate Babe's presence, making sure the physical dynamics felt right for our rehearsal.

grounded_facts: Longfellow uses the butler as a stand-in for Babe to test and refine the physical intimacy of the seating arrangement.
memories.memory_text: I had the butler sit across from me and adjust his posture—telling him to slink lower and move forward—so he could stand in for Babe while I fine-tuned how close and intimate the seating would feel.

grounded_facts: Longfellow tells the butler not to touch anything and to leave the setup exactly as it is before leaving for his bedroom.
memories.memory_text: I remember that Longfellow tells the butler not to touch anything and to leave the setup exactly as it is before leaving for his bedroom.

grounded_facts: Longfellow meticulously adjusts the table setting and instructs butlers to modify the flowers and food in anticipation of Babe's arrival.
memories.memory_text: I carefully adjusted the entire table setting, giving instructions to the butlers about the flowers and food, making sure everything was perfect for Babe's arrival.

grounded_facts: After finalizing the dining setup, Longfellow exits to his bedroom, leaving instructions for the scene to remain untouched.
memories.memory_text: I remember that After finalizing the dining setup, Longfellow exits to his bedroom, leaving instructions for the scene to remain untouched.

grounded_facts: Upon hearing the accusation, Longfellow grabs Cobb by the shirt-front, ready to strangle him in rage.
memories.memory_text: When I heard Cobb’s accusation, I rushed at him and grabbed him by the shirt-front, ready to strangle him in rage.

grounded_facts: Longfellow discovers that Mary Dawson is actually Babe Bennett, a star reporter who has been using him for stories, including coining his 'Cinderella Man' nickname.
memories.memory_text: I was told that Mary Dawson is actually Babe Bennett, the star reporter from The Mail, who's been using me for stories and even gave me that 'Cinderella Man' nickname as part of her act.

grounded_facts: Cobb confronts Longfellow, accusing him of being duped by Babe Bennett (posing as Mary Dawson) and exposing her true identity and intentions.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Cobb that Mary Dawson was actually Babe Bennett, a star reporter on The Mail who had been using me for stories, and that she was the one who gave me the nickname 'Cinderella Man'—he said I’d been making love to a double dose of cyanide.

grounded_facts: Cobb transfers the phone to Longfellow so he can take the call.
memories.memory_text: I remember Cobb handing me the phone so I could take the call.

grounded_facts: Longfellow receives a phone call via Cobb's relay.
Longfellow initiates spoken contact with Mary upon receiving the call.
memories.memory_text: I received a phone call from Mary, and I said 'Hello, Mary?' when I started speaking to her.

grounded_facts: Babe initially greets the caller affectionately, then abruptly changes expression upon recognizing Longfellow's voice.
memories.memory_text: I heard Babe's tone shift suddenly when she recognized my voice—her warmth vanished and her expression went dead.

grounded_facts: Longfellow confronts someone over the phone, accusing them of writing articles about him.
memories.memory_text: I confronted someone over the phone, asking them if they were the one writing those articles about me.

grounded_facts: Longfellow ends a phone call from Babe, after which his emotional state shifts dramatically.
memories.memory_text: I hung up the phone after talking to Babe, and I felt everything inside me change—I could see the truth now, and all my illusions were gone.

grounded_facts: Cobb regrets having delivered news that caused Longfellow's emotional collapse and apologizes indirectly.
memories.memory_text: I saw Cobb look at me and say, 'If I knew you were going to take it so hard, I woulda kept my mouth shut. Sorry,' and I knew he regretted telling me what he did.

grounded_facts: After a period of silence and emotional processing, Longfellow instructs Walter to pack his things and announces he is going home.
memories.memory_text: After sitting in silence and letting everything sink in, I told Walter to pack my things because I decided it was time to go home.

grounded_facts: Longfellow exits his bedroom wearing coat and hat, moving briskly toward the staircase, indicating a decisive departure.
memories.memory_text: I emerged from my bedroom wearing my coat and hat, walking briskly toward the staircase, ready to leave as Cobb and Walter followed me with the luggage.

grounded_facts: Cobb attempts to keep up with Longfellow and questions his decision to leave, expressing concern over the fate of the Estate.
memories.memory_text: Cobb questioned my decision to leave and expressed worry about what would happen to the Estate.

grounded_facts: Cobb tries to keep up with Longfellow and criticizes his departure as irresponsible.
memories.memory_text: I remember Cobb trying to keep up with me, criticizing my departure as irresponsible.

grounded_facts: Longfellow explicitly dismisses any concern for the Estate, indicating he no longer cares about its fate.
memories.memory_text: I made it clear that I no longer cared about the Estate's fate, dismissing any concern for what would happen to it.

grounded_facts: In response to Cobb's concern, Longfellow declares that others can take the Estate, showing detachment.
memories.memory_text: I told Cobb they could have the Estate, showing my detachment and declaring that I no longer felt responsible for it.

grounded_facts: As they approach the staircase, a disturbance is heard, prompting Cobb to move ahead to investigate.
memories.memory_text: As I walked toward the staircase with Cobb and Walter, I heard a commotion from the stairs and saw Cobb hurry ahead to see what was going on.

grounded_facts: A distressed farmer breaks into Longfellow's foyer, demanding to confront him about his wealth and indifference to the suffering of others.
An uninvited farmer forces his way into Longfellow's home and confronts him publicly in the grand foyer.
memories.memory_text: I saw a wild-eyed farmer break into my foyer, struggling with my butlers as he shouted that he wanted to see me, and he finally stared at me, saying he just wanted to know what kind of man I was.

grounded_facts: Longfellow dismisses the farmer as a moocher, rejecting his plea and moral argument.
memories.memory_text: I told that farmer he was a moocher, just like all the rest, and I told him to get out of here—I didn't believe a word he said, not even on a stack of bibles.

grounded_facts: The farmer directly accuses Longfellow of selfishness and moral blindness for spending lavishly while others starve.
memories.memory_text: I heard the farmer accuse me of being selfish and blind, yelling that I spent thousands on parties while people starve, and he mocked me for feeding doughnuts to a horse instead of helping families in need.

grounded_facts: After being restrained, the farmer suddenly produces a gun, threatens Cobb, then points it at Longfellow, escalating the confrontation.
memories.memory_text: I saw the farmer pull a gun after being restrained—he pointed it at Cobb and then at me, and I just stood there, frozen, while he stared at the weapon like he didn't even know how it got into his hand.

grounded_facts: The farmer reveals his personal suffering—losing his farm, feeding his children, pride in work—and pleads for understanding.
memories.memory_text: He told me he just wanted a chance to feed his wife and kids, reminded me my money wouldn't help when I'm six feet under, and spoke of years of hard work lost—how his kids went hungry and his proud wife kept saying everything would be all right.

grounded_facts: The farmer, overwhelmed by despair, lowers his gun and collapses into sobs, expressing regret and hopelessness.
memories.memory_text: The farmer broke down in front of me—sobbing, dropping his gun, and confessing he was at the end of his rope, overwhelmed by losing his farm and failing to feed his family.

grounded_facts: Longfellow silently watches the farmer's emotional collapse with growing pity, marking a shift in his perception.
memories.memory_text: I watched him closely as he spoke, saying nothing, but I felt my anger fade and pity take hold—seeing the truth in his pain changed something in me.

grounded_facts: A quiet meal between the man and Longfellow at a table set for Babe, marked by minimal dialogue and deep contemplation.
memories.memory_text: I sat across from the man during a quiet meal, watching him eat while I remained lost in thought, the silence between us heavy with unspoken things.

grounded_facts: The man tentatively asks Longfellow if he can take leftover food home, showing deference or uncertainty about the rules of the setting.
The man at the table tentatively asks Longfellow if he can take some food with him after eating.
memories.memory_text: I remember the man looking up and asking me, 'Can I take some of this home with me?'—his voice tentative, as if he wasn't sure he had the right to ask.

grounded_facts: Newspaper headlines disclose that Longfellow (Deeds) plans to give away his fortune by dividing a large farming district into small, fully equipped farms for the unemployed.
memories.memory_text: I remember seeing the newspaper headlines announcing that I planned to give away my fortune by dividing a large farming district into small, fully equipped farms for the unemployed.

grounded_facts: Longfellow asks the applicant if he is married and whether he has children as part of the hiring assessment.
memories.memory_text: I asked the applicant if he was married and whether he had children to help assess his suitability for the job.

memories.memory_text: I approved Mr. Dodsworth for employment and told him to take my note to another desk for further instructions.

grounded_facts: A structured employment screening event where Longfellow interviews applicants in his transformed drawing room.
memories.memory_text: I was sitting in my drawing room, which we'd turned into a hiring station, with a line of men waiting to be interviewed and one applicant in front of me at a time.

grounded_facts: Longfellow asks how many applicants he has approved; the clerk reports 819, which Longfellow finds insufficient given the pace.
memories.memory_text: I asked how many applicants I had approved so far, and when I heard it was 819, I thought that was too few—we need more workers and the pace is too slow.

grounded_facts: Longfellow takes a phone call regarding water development and road layout, approves water plans but requests a meeting to review maps of the road layout.
memories.memory_text: I took a phone call about the water and road plans; I approved the water development but told them to come back tonight at ten with the maps so I could review the road layout because I wasn't satisfied with it yet.

grounded_facts: A routine business update involving delivery of a plow order and discussion of operational logistics.
memories.memory_text: I received the plow order and was told we got a good price, and I said I'd look it over later.

grounded_facts: The farmer tells Longfellow that his wife prays for him every night, expressing personal admiration.
The farmer delivers an order for plows and informs Longfellow that his wife prays for him every night, causing visible embarrassment.
memories.memory_text: I was told by a farmer that his wife prays for me every night, and I remember feeling a bit embarrassed while he delivered his plow order.

grounded_facts: Cobb angrily refuses a sales offer to buy bulls and asserts that he is a seller, not a buyer.
Cobb receives a call about buying bulls, angrily refuses, and declares that he has spent his life selling bulls, not buying them.
memories.memory_text: I was on the phone when someone tried to sell me bulls, but I told them no — I've spent my whole life selling bulls, not buying them, and I made that clear before slamming down the receiver.

grounded_facts: Svenson offers a sandwich to Longfellow when he learns he is having lunch.
memories.memory_text: I remember Svenson offering me a sandwich when he heard I was having lunch, saying, 'If you like to have a sandwich, I can give you one, please.'

grounded_facts: Longfellow orders lunch for the waiting applicants after accepting a sandwich from one of them.
memories.memory_text: After accepting the sandwich, I told Cobb, 'Get lunch for the rest of them,' because I wanted to make sure the others waiting weren't left out.

grounded_facts: An applicant spokesman expresses collective admiration and hope inspired by Longfellow.
memories.memory_text: I remember the applicant spokesman telling me that the boys thought I was swell and that I gave them hope, which meant a lot to me in that moment.

grounded_facts: Longfellow is served with an insanity warrant and taken into custody by deputy sheriffs.
memories.memory_text: I was served with an insanity warrant and taken into custody by the deputy sheriffs, who said I had to come along with them, though they mentioned it was only temporary until a hearing.

grounded_facts: Charlie reveals he represents the complainant and that the legal action stems from concerns about Longfellow giving away money.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Charlie that he represented the complainant and that the legal action was because people were concerned about me giving away the money from the estate.

grounded_facts: Deputy sheriff asserts authority by demanding compliance and using dismissive language.
memories.memory_text: I remember the deputy sheriff asserting his authority, telling me we were wasting time and that I had to go with them, speaking in a way that felt dismissive.

grounded_facts: Longfellow violently pushes away the deputies when they grab his arms, then agrees to go peacefully.
memories.memory_text: When the deputies grabbed my arms, I pushed them away violently at first, but then I decided to go peacefully.

grounded_facts: A public gathering of farmers and others waiting to meet Longfellow, who is receiving them in his drawing room.
memories.memory_text: I saw a crowd of farmers and others gathered, waiting to meet me in my drawing room, and I noticed some pushing and murmuring among them as one man was brought forward.

grounded_facts: Cobb shares a personal story of romantic betrayal to build rapport and encourage Longfellow to regain fighting spirit.
memories.memory_text: I recall Cobb sharing a story about a woman in Syracuse who betrayed him, saying he came out of it full of fight, and he told me not to give up now.

grounded_facts: Cobb attempts to motivate Longfellow to resist the legal framing and psychiatric accusation he faces, warning of the consequences of passivity.
memories.memory_text: I saw Cobb pacing and confronting me, urging me to stop sitting back and letting them frame me, warning me about the prosecution's power and how I'd be ruined if I didn't fight back.

grounded_facts: Cobb explicitly informs Longfellow that the prosecution aims to declare him insane and institutionalize him, urging resistance.
memories.memory_text: I remember Cobb telling me that they were trying to prove I'm insane so they could lock me up in the bughouse if they won the case, and he urged me to fight it.

grounded_facts: Babe impulsively starts to rise upon seeing Longfellow, but Mac stops her with a hand.
memories.memory_text: I saw Babe start to get up when she saw me, but Mac stopped her with his hand.

grounded_facts: Longfellow arrives in the courtroom accompanied by his guard, drawing immediate attention from everyone present.
memories.memory_text: I entered the courtroom with my guard, and I could feel everyone's eyes on me, but I didn't look left or right—I just kept my gaze forward and sat down, slumping in the chair as I stared into space.

grounded_facts: Cobb informs Longfellow that Cedar wants to make a settlement, offering him a chance to escape the legal proceedings, but receives no response.
Cobb excitedly tells Longfellow that Cedar wants to make a settlement and asks for his response.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Cobb that Cedar wanted to make a settlement and give me a chance to get out of the mess, and he asked what I would say, but I didn't respond.

grounded_facts: The judge formally asks Longfellow whether he is represented by counsel.
memories.memory_text: I remember the judge asking me directly, 'Are you represented by counsel, Mr. Deeds?' while looking at me from the bench.

grounded_facts: A formal court proceeding to assess Longfellow Deeds' mental competence, held in the Supreme Court of New York County.
memories.memory_text: I was told this was a hearing about my sanity, and the judge asked if I had a lawyer, which I don't, and whether I wanted to defend myself, even though I already know I won't.

grounded_facts: The judge notes that Longfellow has no legal representation and shows no intention to defend himself, then allows the hearing to proceed.
memories.memory_text: I heard the judge note that I had no lawyer and wasn't planning to defend myself, and then I heard him say 'Proceed.'

grounded_facts: Cedar formally requests to call Babe Bennett as the first witness in the hearing to prove Longfellow Deeds' insanity.
memories.memory_text: I saw Cedar stand up and formally call Babe Bennett as the first witness against me, right there in the courtroom.

grounded_facts: After Babe's outburst, the Judge warns her of arrest and orders her removal from the stand for disrupting court order.
memories.memory_text: After Babe spoke out, I saw the judge warn her that she'd be arrested if she kept disrupting the court, and he ordered her to sit down.

grounded_facts: Cedar questions Babe about her employment and authorship of articles on Deeds, attempting to establish credibility for the prosecution's case.
memories.memory_text: I watched as Cedar questioned Babe about her job at the Morning Mail and whether she wrote those articles about me, trying to make them seem credible.

grounded_facts: Babe, under oath, openly defies Cedar's questioning by rejecting the truth of her own articles and accusing the court of a frameup.
Babe directly challenges the legitimacy of the hearing, accusing it of being a frameup and demanding to be heard.
memories.memory_text: I heard Babe suddenly shout that the whole hearing was ridiculous and a frameup, and she refused to go along with Cedar's questions, saying I wasn't insane at all.

grounded_facts: A formal legal proceeding in a courtroom to determine whether Longfellow Deeds is mentally fit to manage his inherited fortune, involving witness testimony, expert diagnosis, public sentiment, and moral confrontation.
memories.memory_text: I realized this whole courtroom proceeding was meant to decide if I was mentally fit to handle my inherited fortune, based on testimony and expert claims.

grounded_facts: When asked by the judge if he has anything to say in defense of the allegations, Longfellow Deeds remains silent.
memories.memory_text: When the judge asked me if I had anything to say in defense, I remained silent and just shook my head, even though I could feel the weight of everyone's eyes on me.

grounded_facts: Despite Babe's retraction, Cedar submits her articles as evidence, and the judge marks them Exhibit A for the plaintiff.
memories.memory_text: Even after Babe rejected her own articles, I saw Cedar still hand them to the judge, and I heard the judge mark them as Exhibit A for the plaintiff.

grounded_facts: After Babe is dismissed, Mac places an affectionate arm around her shoulders as she returns to her seat.
memories.memory_text: After Babe was dismissed, I noticed Mac put his arm around her shoulders as she returned to her seat, showing he supported her.

grounded_facts: A psychiatrist clarifies for the court that 'pixilated' is an old American term meaning someone is mentally unbalanced, equivalent to being 'balmy.'
memories.memory_text: I heard the psychiatrist explain to the court that 'pixilated' means someone is mentally unbalanced, like being 'balmy,' because the pixies got them.

grounded_facts: Cedar questions the Falkner sisters about their knowledge of Deeds, guiding them to confirm community belief in his instability.
memories.memory_text: I saw Cedar questioning the Falkner sisters, guiding them to confirm that everyone believes I'm unstable, as if he already decided what the truth should be.

grounded_facts: The Falkner sisters collectively testify that the townspeople believe Longfellow Deeds is 'pixilated,' citing his odd behaviors such as walking in the rain without a hat, talking to himself, and violently confronting Chuck Dillon.
memories.memory_text: I heard the Falkner sisters say in court that people back home think I'm 'pixilated' because I walk in the rain without a hat, talk to myself, and had a violent run-in with Chuck Dillon.

grounded_facts: A series of witnesses — including a policeman, waiter, Madame Pomponi, bodyguards, and a cabman — recount incidents where Deeds acted unpredictably, such as cleaning a restaurant, ejecting performers, dismissing bodyguards, and feeding doughnuts to a horse.
memories.memory_text: I remember the waiter testifying that I was mopping the floor, and the bodyguards saying I threw them out — people kept recounting how I acted in ways they didn't expect, like feeding doughnuts to a horse.

grounded_facts: Cedar presents photographic enlargements of Deeds's antics and has them authenticated by the photographer.
Cedar presents enlarged photographs of Deeds engaging in unusual behavior, authenticated by Bob, the photographer who took the original images.
memories.memory_text: I saw Cedar present enlarged photos of me doing odd things, and the photographer named Bob confirmed he took them, saying he often photographs people others call 'nuts'.

grounded_facts: Dr. Emil Von Holler testifies that Longfellow Deeds suffers from manic depression, explaining the condition using a mood chart and linking Deeds's behaviors — such as hosting a reception and then throwing guests out — to mood cycles.
Dr. Von Holler uses a mood chart to explain manic depression and applies it directly to Deeds's behavior, asserting he is mentally ill.
memories.memory_text: I watched Dr. Von Holler testify that I suffer from manic depression, using a mood chart to explain my behavior and saying outright that I'm 'verrukt'.

grounded_facts: After presenting all evidence and expert testimony, Cedar formally concludes the prosecution's presentation in the insanity hearing.
memories.memory_text: I remember when Cedar finished presenting all the evidence and simply said, 'Your Honor, we rest,' marking the end of the prosecution's case.

grounded_facts: Babe leans close to Longfellow and pleads with him to speak, expressing remorse and love.
memories.memory_text: I remember Babe leaning close to me, pleading softly, telling me she knew how horrible she'd been and begging me to speak, saying it would mean everything if I did it for her.

grounded_facts: Babe Bennett interrupts the court's decision process, insisting that Longfellow Deeds must be given a chance to defend himself before being committed.
memories.memory_text: I was sitting in court, feeling resigned, when suddenly Babe Bennett stood up and shouted that I couldn't be committed without being given a chance to speak — she insisted I must be allowed to defend myself.

grounded_facts: Babe Bennett testifies that Deeds is not insane but has been victimized by the press and herself, arguing that his honesty makes him appear crazy in a corrupt world.
memories.memory_text: I heard Babe testify that I'm not insane, that I've been hurt by everyone since I arrived—especially her—and that the press twisted my words to make me look foolish; she said my honesty makes me seem crazy in a world that can't handle it.

grounded_facts: Mac, Babe's editor, confirms that Babe quit her job out of respect for Deeds and endorses her account, adding institutional credibility.
Mac publicly backs Babe's account and affirms Deeds's character, nudging Deeds to speak.
memories.memory_text: I remember Mac, Babe's editor, standing up and telling the court that Babe quit her job because she thought I was a swell fellow, and he backed up everything she said; then he looked right at me and urged me not to be a sucker and to stand up and speak my piece.

grounded_facts: Cedar attempts to discredit Babe by claiming she is in love with Deeds; Babe defiantly admits it but insists it doesn't invalidate her truth.
memories.memory_text: I was in the courtroom when Cedar tried to undermine Babe by saying she was in love with me, and she defiantly admitted it, shouting 'Yes!!!'—I could feel how much she meant it, and how she still stood by the truth despite the attack.

grounded_facts: Farmers and townspeople in the audience rise up, demanding that Deeds speak and declaring their support, showing collective solidarity.
memories.memory_text: I saw the farmers and townspeople in the audience rise up, shouting at me—'How about us, Mr. Deeds!'—demanding that I speak and declaring their support, showing they stood with me.

grounded_facts: Longfellow defends normalcy by pointing out common 'odd' behaviors like doodling and O-filling, using the Judge and Dr. Von Holler as examples.
memories.memory_text: I pointed out how the Judge fills in O's when thinking and said that everyone has little habits like that—doodling or playing the tuba helps us concentrate, and I don't see anything wrong with it.

grounded_facts: Longfellow exposes Dr. Von Holler's doodling as a 'foolish' habit, undermining his expert status by equating it with tuba playing.
memories.memory_text: I noticed Dr. Von Holler was doodling during the trial, so I picked up his paper and said he makes foolish little drawings too, just like tuba playing—it's nothing to be called crazy over.

grounded_facts: Longfellow uses a doodle of Mr. Cedar to illustrate that everyone, including authority figures, engages in odd behaviors, normalizing his own eccentricities.
Longfellow hands a doodle resembling Cedar to the judge, inviting ridicule and undermining Cedar's dignity.
memories.memory_text: I handed my doodle of Mr. Cedar to the judge and said it was Exhibit A for the defense, pointing out how everyone has their quirks—like Dr. Von Holler doodling to think, or Semple twitching his nose—because I wanted to show that my own habits aren't crazy, just human.

grounded_facts: Longfellow acknowledges being drunk during past incidents, attributing his actions to a one-time lapse rather than insanity.
memories.memory_text: I admitted to the court that I was drunk during those incidents, and that’s why I don’t remember them—it was the first time I’d ever been drunk, and I explained it as something that could happen to anyone.

grounded_facts: Longfellow points out that Cedar's son was also drunk and acted recklessly, undermining Cedar's moral authority.
Longfellow directly questions Cedar about his son's drunken behavior, challenging his moral standing.
memories.memory_text: I pointed out to Mr. Cedar that his son had also gotten drunk and recklessly driven a taxi, and I directly asked him if that wasn't true, challenging his right to judge me.

grounded_facts: Longfellow confirms that the Falkner sisters live rent-free in a house he owns, demonstrating generosity and undermining claims of irrationality.
memories.memory_text: I asked Jane and Amy who owned their house, and they confirmed I did — then I reminded them they pay no rent, which shows I’m supporting them out of kindness.

grounded_facts: Longfellow asks Jane who in Mandrake Falls is 'pixilated,' leading to the conclusion that everyone is except the sisters themselves.
memories.memory_text: I asked Jane who in Mandrake Falls was pixilated, and she said everyone except the two of them, which made me realize how unfairly people judge others’ behavior.

grounded_facts: Longfellow explains his desire to distribute his wealth as an effort to help struggling people, framing it as moral responsibility rather than madness.
memories.memory_text: I explained that I want to use my money to help the people who can't make it on their own, like those struggling to get over the hill — it's not madness, it's just the right thing to do.

grounded_facts: Longfellow calls on applicants for farms to stand, visually demonstrating who he intends to help.
memories.memory_text: I called on all the men who applied for farms to stand up, so everyone could see exactly who I'm trying to help — those fellows need the chance I have.

grounded_facts: Longfellow outlines his structured plan to give land and resources to struggling families, framing it as rational and morally justified.
memories.memory_text: I remember explaining my plan in court—how I intended to give ten acres, a horse, a cow, and some seed to each family, and if they worked the farm for three years, the land would be theirs. I stood by it, believing it was rational and fair.

grounded_facts: Longfellow claims Cedar does not genuinely believe he is insane, pointing out that Cedar offered to drop the case if financially compensated, thus revealing self-interest over concern for public welfare.
memories.memory_text: I told them that Cedar doesn't really think I'm insane—he proved that when he offered to drop the case if I paid him off, so his concern isn't public welfare, it's personal gain.

grounded_facts: Cedar interrupts the proceedings to call Longfellow's proposal 'colossally stupid' and an 'insult to intelligence,' escalating personal conflict.
memories.memory_text: I remember Cedar shouting that my plan was a lie, calling it 'colossally stupid' and an insult to intelligence, which felt like a personal attack meant to humiliate me.

grounded_facts: After remaining silent, Longfellow Deeds finally speaks up, requesting to give his side of the story in response to the public support and Babe's plea.
memories.memory_text: I finally spoke up in court because of Babe's plea and seeing so many people support me; I told the judge I wanted to give my side, even if it didn't change anything.

grounded_facts: Longfellow physically assaults Cedar after accusing him of hypocrisy and attempting to block his philanthropic plan, marking a climactic breakdown of decorum and restraint.
memories.memory_text: After he insulted me and tried to destroy my plan, I got up and punched Cedar in the jaw—I couldn't hold back anymore.

grounded_facts: The judge delivers the final verdict in Mr. Deeds' sanity hearing, concluding the trial.
memories.memory_text: I sat in court as the judge began speaking, noting how the tone of his words made me fear the worst after all the damaging testimony he mentioned.

grounded_facts: The judge declares Mr. Deeds sane and dismisses the case, reversing the expected outcome.
memories.memory_text: I could hardly believe it when the judge declared me not only sane but the sanest man he'd ever seen in his courtroom, then dismissed the case.

grounded_facts: The judge publicly acknowledges Longfellow's role by clasping his hand after the verdict.
memories.memory_text: I felt a surge of warmth when the judge smiled at me and clasped my hand, a gesture that meant more than just acquittal.

grounded_facts: Mrs. Semple slaps her husband in anger after the verdict goes against their interests.
memories.memory_text: I saw Mrs. Semple turn and slap her husband right after the verdict, clearly furious that their plan had failed.

grounded_facts: Budington confronts Cedar, accusing him of orchestrating a failed scheme.
memories.memory_text: I watched Budington stand up and confront Cedar, shouting that he knew about the scheme, blaming him for everything falling apart.

grounded_facts: After the verdict, Longfellow is lifted and carried out by jubilant farmers and supporters.
memories.memory_text: I was lifted up by the farmers and carried out on their shoulders, surrounded by a jubilant crowd right after the verdict.

grounded_facts: Babe is unable to reach Longfellow and is left alone in the courtroom after the crowd departs.
memories.memory_text: I was carried away by the crowd celebrating me, and I couldn't see Babe or reach her—I didn't even know she was trying to get through until later.

grounded_facts: Longfellow breaks away from the crowd, returns to the courtroom, and reunites with Babe.
memories.memory_text: I broke away from the crowd and returned to the courtroom to find Babe, looking around a little dazed as I finally reached her.

grounded_facts: Longfellow returns to the courtroom and sweeps Babe into his arms, leading to a passionate embrace.
memories.memory_text: I ran to Babe and swept her up in my arms, and when she kissed me over and over, I gave her one passionate kiss back.

memories.memory_text: I flicked the string again and again, feeling the rhythm in my fingers until finally the knot snapped tight—just as the last reporter passed by. I didn’t look up, but I knew he saw it.

I asked for a month’s vacation—with pay—right after Mac said I could have anything for the story, and then I told him to leave four columns open on the front page. I didn’t raise my voice, but I felt it—the shift.
I saw him through the taxi window—there he was, just standing there, and I knew it was him. I pointed and said, 'There he is. Yep, that's him.'
I turned to the photographers and told them to get ready—'Get the cameras ready and follow me.' I didn’t explain, just gave the order and meant to move fast.

I reached the tree and clutched it, letting myself crumple down—just in time to see his eyes widen. When he lifted my head, I opened my eyes slowly, pretending to be dazed, and whispered, 'Oh, did I? I'm sorry...'
I flipped the coin in my hand, making it vanish when he wasn't looking—Mac was too caught up in the story to notice, too busy calling me a genius and saying he could kiss me.

I remember sitting up on that bus, watching Longfellow take it all in—the city lights, the way his face lit up when he talked about the Aquarium. I just said, 'I enjoy it,' but it was more than that. I liked being the one showing him around.

I asked him what they said about the opera, and he just looked at me and said they thought he was crazy, like he wanted to run it like a grocery store—then he started talking about my hair instead, like it didn’t matter.

I heard those girls laugh and say 'Cinderella Man!' like it was a joke, and I couldn't look up—I felt it in my chest, how they were mocking him, and then he said it too, quiet, like he was already expecting it.
I asked him what he saw at Grant's Tomb, and then I watched his face as he spoke—really watched him—and for once, I couldn’t laugh, even though part of me wanted to.
I laughed when he tried to spit down on Times Square, but then I had to wipe his coat—his question caught me off guard, and I could feel the guilt rising before I even answered.
I reminded him he once called me a lady in distress—such an odd thing to say, but it stayed with me, like he saw something no one else did.
I asked if he was engaged, and when he said no, there was a pause. Then I asked if he didn't go out with girls much, and he said he hadn't.
We were laughing together, really laughing, and then suddenly he was gone—just ran off toward the siren without looking back, leaving me sitting there alone with my voice still hanging in the air.
I couldn't type another word—my hands just froze, and all I could do was rest my forehead on the typewriter, like if I pressed hard enough, I might disappear.
I told him I couldn't sleep either, and it felt like the first honest thing I'd said in weeks—just two words, but they hung there, heavy and real.
I said I'd like to read it some time, and for a moment, I really meant it—his voice on the phone, talking about a poem for me, made something inside me shift, even though he called her Mary.
I said it out loud—'I'm crucifying him'—and the words caught in my throat like something I couldn't swallow.
I remember saying he was wholesome, fresh, that he wanted to carry his bride over the threshold—then realizing, 'He's got goodness, Mabel,' like I'd forgotten what that even meant.
I overheard a man say that someone still believes in Santa Claus, and the others laughed.
I just couldn't stand seeing him again—I folded my things so carefully, like if I did it right, the ache might quiet down, but it didn’t.
I told them we weren't going out tonight—just said it flat, like it didn’t matter. My voice didn’t even shake.
After Mabel opened the door and he stood there—so serious, asking for me—I felt my throat tighten. I don’t know why I said it, but I asked if he wanted to go for a walk.
Mac’s eyes lit up when I told him Longfellow proposed—like it was just another headline, another story to sell. I could see the words forming in his mind before he even spoke them.
I said I’d tell Longfellow the truth at lunch, and even though I’m sure he’ll throw me out, I have to try. Walking away from Mac’s office, I knew there was no other way.

I handed Mac my little black book with all the headwaiters' names, and when he begged me to stay, I just shook my head—no words, just the finality of it. The phone rang right after, and I picked it up, but I already knew I wouldn’t be coming back.
I said 'Oh, hello darling' before I even saw him properly, and then my face just froze—realizing it was Longfellow, not Cobb, standing there.

I was trying to explain myself to Longfellow on the phone, stalling, saying I was coming up to talk—but then my voice just stopped. I couldn’t make the words come out, not with him listening like that.
I asked the guard to just say my name, and when he told me the man inside goes wild at the sound of it, I felt the words hit me like a slap—I flinched before I could stop myself.
I sat there and then saw him walk in, so still and far away—I couldn't help but start to stand, to reach toward him somehow, but Mac held me back.
I stood up in that courtroom and shouted the truth, even though the judge threatened me—I couldn't stay silent while they twisted everything to hurt him.

I heard Mrs. Meredith say Deeds makes most of his money from poetry, not the Tallow Works, and that he got $25 for one postcard poem, which she read aloud.
I couldn't find Longfellow anywhere, and with the train coming and the band already playing, I started to fear he'd backed out completely.
Just as the song was ending, Cobb grabbed my arm and pointed—there he was, playing tuba in the band, completely out of place but right on time.
I stood beside Longfellow on the observation platform as the train began to move, the band playing 'Auld Lang Syne' behind us, the crowd shouting farewells and shoving fruit into his hands.
I offered Longfellow a cigar and told him not to worry, that he could leave everything to me—I would handle his responsibilities.
I walked in and asked the secretary where they were—no time for pleasantries, they needed to see me right away.
I didn't get the Power of Attorney from Deeds last night, but I told my associates not to worry—I made it clear I would get it, just like I did with old man Semple.
When I asked Deeds what he planned to do with the money, he said, 'I guess I'd give it away'—I remember the way my brothers laughed, but I saw the opportunity in his naivety.

I offered to handle everything for Longfellow Deeds without extra charge, presenting it as a generous service from our firm, but he immediately questioned why there would be no cost—just like the others who tried to get close to him.
I stood there with Hallor, smiling politely when Longfellow mocked the tailcoat, maintaining a composed presence even as he rejected the symbols of the world he’s now part of.
I snapped at Budington and cut him off—another week gone and still no Power of Attorney from Deeds. I can't strangle the man, but this delay is unbearable.
I heard 'nuisance value' and suddenly saw it—not a bother, but a weapon. I opened the door myself and called in the Semples, smoothing it over like they were important clients.
I pressed the dictagraph button the moment Semple began to sign, and I told Charlie we were off—papers all set?—then ordered him to subpoena the newspaper writer immediately.
Cobb kept shouting at me, saying Cedar was too smart and that I was cooked unless I fought back, but I couldn't bring myself to respond.
I declared that Deeds should be confined to an institution, and the newspapers carried my words—this hearing will set the record straight on his incompetence.
I stood inside the railing with my assistants and the psychiatrists, arranging our papers as the courtroom filled and the spectators buzzed with anticipation.

I presented Babe Bennett as my first witness, certain her articles would prove Deeds' instability, but when she stood there with that reporter beside her, I knew her loyalty to him might undermine everything.
I allowed myself a small grimace of satisfaction, certain the Judge’s stern warning meant he would rule against Deeds and uphold my case.

memories.memory_text: I stood with the band, playing my tuba as we performed 'For He's a Jolly Good Fellow'—not as the guest of honor, just another player in the row.
I saw Cobb point and grab Cedar’s arm—something in his stare made me realize they’d just recognized me, though I hadn’t meant to be seen.
I remember seeing that tuxedo and thinking it looked like a monkey suit—something ridiculous, not for me. I told Walter right away I'd never worn anything like that and didn't plan to start now.
I remember turning down the opera people's request for $180,000 without hesitation, and when Hallor pressed me about his client, I could tell he was just after something more. I didn't trust him.

I slid down the banister after leaving my room, just to move quietly and maybe shake off whoever might be watching—then touched the statue at the bottom, a small habit, like a quiet wish before trying to make it out the door.

I asked the bodyguards to fetch a trunk from a closet, and the moment they stepped inside, I closed the door and locked it—calmly, without rushing—then walked out whistling, knowing they couldn’t follow.
Morrow, swaying and half-drunk, told me to sock him right on the chin, offering to eat a pack of my postcards raw if I would just hit him — like he needed punishment for being a skunk.
He said I was his guest forever, then offered to take me on a binge through New York, promising to show me sights I'd never seen and introduce me to every wit, nit-wit, and half-wit in the city.

I heard those girls laughing as they passed, calling me 'Cinderella Man' like it was some kind of joke—'the dope!'—and I just sat there, feeling my face burn, wanting to knock their heads together if they were men.

I looked at Babe after they left, waiting for her to say something—anything—but she stayed silent, wouldn't meet my eyes, and when I brought up the papers, she just changed the subject like she couldn't stand to talk about it.
I stood there looking at Grant's Tomb and felt it—how an ordinary farm boy could rise to lead an army, help save a nation, and become President. That kind of thing only happens in America.
I got so caught up in what I was saying that my voice tightened and I nearly choked—then I had to stop and say 'Excuse me' like I'd made a mistake.

I tried to spit down into Times Square, but the wind blew it back on my coat, and Babe had to wipe it off with her handkerchief while laughing—it felt breezy, and then she asked if I was worried about the articles, but I could see she wasn’t entirely honest when I asked if she believed them.
I was singing with Babe, laughing like I hadn’t in a long time, when I heard the siren—low at first, then louder. I jumped up without thinking and ran toward the street, calling back for her to wait.

I hopped onto the fire engine and gave a short salute, saying I was Captain Deeds, fire volunteer from Mandrake Falls. One of the firefighters laughed and called out, 'Hi, Cap! Boys, meet the Captain!'
I told Babe I’d been writing a poem about her because it’s hard for me to say things out loud—so I write them.

I shouted from the top of the stairs and heard the echo bounce back—it felt sharp and clean, like the space was answering me. When Walter hesitated, I told him to try it, then insisted he go louder until the sound filled the staircase.

I pointed to each servant as if conducting a choir, bringing their hoots and shrieks together into one crashing wave of noise. After the burst, I declared it a lesson and walked away, knowing the silence afterward made it feel like something real had happened.

I told her I waited in the park for over an hour, and when she said she didn’t think I could come, I told her I threw the guests out—just like that. Mabel looked shocked, like I’d grabbed them by the neck, but I didn’t care.

After I said I didn’t mind the scandal, she suddenly asked if I wanted to go for a walk. I said yes—hesitant, not sure if it was too late—and then she went to get her hat, and everything felt different.

I told Mary I'm going home in a day or so—walking through the fog, I just knew I didn't fit here, not with all the noise and rushing around. I wanted to talk, to make her understand why I had to leave.
I asked Mary if I could talk to her. I told her I used to hike in the woods back home and talk to an imaginary girl, show her my pet trees.

I remember adjusting the flowers on the table—lifting the big bowl away and asking for a smaller one so I could actually see across the table. It mattered that I wouldn’t be looking at a wall of petals when she sat down.
I made sure they had plenty of that pâté—what I called the 'goo' that tastes like soap—because I knew Babe liked it. I told the butler to have a lot ready, like it was something important.
I turned when I heard the name, and something in Cobb’s voice made my blood run cold—I grabbed him by the shirt, demanding to know what he was talking about, ready to fight him right then.
I saw the photo in the newspaper Cobb held up—Babe Bennett, not Mary Dawson—and I just went numb; I took the paper and sat on the bed, staring at it, unable to believe I’d been fooled.
I picked up the phone and asked her directly—my voice tight—'Is it you who's been writing those articles about me?'
I hung up the phone after Babe's voice came through, and I couldn't feel anything—just a hollow silence, like all the pieces inside me had broken and fallen away.
I walked out of my bedroom, down the hall toward the stairs, with Cobb and Walter behind me—Walter struggling under all those suitcases. I said, 'They can have the Estate,' and meant it.
I watched that farmer break down, his voice cracking as he talked about his kids going hungry and standing in bread lines—I saw the gun in his hand, then on the floor, and all I could feel was pity.
He said 'I guess I'm at the end of my rope' in a barely audible voice, then sobbed openly. I watched him closely and saw him hide his face in his hands.
I remember the way he looked up, hesitant, asking if he could take some food home—just a simple question, but it stayed with me.

I was sitting at my desk, tired and unshaven, asking applicant after applicant the same questions—'Are you married? Any children?'—and by the time I'd approved 819, it still felt like we weren't moving fast enough.

The farmer told me his wife prays for me every night, and I didn’t know what to say—just mumbled thanks before quickly turning to the next man, George Rankin, as if shifting focus could hide how much it unsettled me.

Cobb was pacing and then suddenly turned to me, raising his voice, saying I was being framed and that they’d put me in the bughouse if I didn’t fight—his voice got softer when he pleaded, like he actually cared, but I couldn’t bring myself to answer.
I walked in with the guard, kept my eyes down, and didn't answer when the judge asked if I had a lawyer—I just sat there, slumped in the chair, staring ahead.

I remember seeing the Falkner sisters come in, trembling and whispering to each other, and I smiled at them—just like I always did back home—but then I heard one of them say I was 'pixilated,' and the word hung in the air like it was supposed to mean something more than just odd or different.

I sat there, my heart pounding, as the Judge spoke about the strange things people had said about me—my behavior, the tuba, the rhymes—everything laid bare, and I could feel the weight of it pressing down, wondering if they’d finally decide I didn’t belong in this world on my own terms.

Before the verdict came, I stole a quick look toward where Babe was sitting—just a glance, furtive and quiet—hoping for some sign, some anchor, though I didn’t dare speak or move, trapped between the gavel and the silence.
